(Nasdaq: NN) is a Reston, Virginia-based technology company that has spent nearly two decades engineering a terrestrial alternative to satellite GPS for indoor, urban-canyon, and GPS-denied environments. Its competitive moat rests on a single durable asset: FCC-licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population, which NextNav is seeking to consolidate into a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use block capable of hosting 5G NR Positioning Reference Signals. The company's flagship commercial product — Pinnacle — provides floor-level altitude determination for Enhanced 911 calls across 4,400-plus U.S. cities, deployed through AT&T's FirstNet network and generating the bulk of NextNav's $4–6 million annual revenue. Its strategic platform — TerraPoiNT — is a ground-based PNT network whose terrestrial signals are roughly 10,000 times stronger than GPS signals at ground level, making them exceptionally resistant to jamming and spoofing. The next-generation 'NextGen' platform embeds PNT capability directly into standard 5G NR infrastructure, a proof-of-concept demonstrated successfully on commercial 5G equipment in October 2025. The investment thesis is a high-conviction regulatory arbitrage: if the FCC approves NextNav's April 2024 Petition for Rulemaking — formalized as WT Docket No. 25-110 in March 2025, with an NPRM noticed to OMB as of early 2026 — NextNav's spectrum holdings transform from a niche E911 revenue stream into the licensed backbone of a national GPS resilience mandate, opening carrier licensing, federal contract, and international royalty revenue streams at a scale orders of magnitude above current levels. The December 2025 MetCom partnership, extending the NextGen waveform license to Japan's largest metro areas, validates international demand. Against this optionality, investors must weigh concentrated revenue risk (one customer, AT&T, represented 89 percent of Q3 2025 revenue), accelerating net losses ($189.3 million in FY 2025), a market capitalization in excess of $2 billion at a price-to-sales ratio above 350x, and execution risk on a technology platform that has not yet been deployed at commercial scale by any mobile network operator. CEO Mariam Sorond, a 30-year wireless-industry veteran with prior roles at VMware, CableLabs, and DISH Network, is steering NextNav through what management characterizes as a once-in-a-generation spectrum policy window.

chapters.title: The Spectrum Bet: NextNav's Strategic Position as of May 2026
chapters.body:
On a spring morning in Reston, Virginia, the market has already rendered its verdict on NextNav Inc. before the trading day opens. The company's shares carry a valuation north of $2 billion. Its annual revenue is $4.6 million — roughly the cost of two mid-tier Washington lobbyists. The gap between those two numbers is not an anomaly or an oversight. It is, in its entirety, a bet on a single docket number at the Federal Communications Commission: WT Docket No. 25-110. Everything else — the engineering, the partnerships, the financing — is prologue.

## Three Pillars, One Thesis

NextNav's strategic position as of May 2026 rests on three interlocking assets that exist nowhere else in the U.S. telecommunications landscape. The first is spectrum: as of September 2025, the company holds ~~12 MHz of contiguous Mobile Location and Monitoring Service (M-LMS) licenses in the 902–928 MHz band, covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population~~ ==a total of 12 MHz of Mobile Location and Monitoring Service (M-LMS) licenses in the 902–928 MHz band — 8 MHz of contiguous spectrum covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population, plus an additional 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering a partial U.S. footprint== — a position assembled over nearly two decades and expanded through a license acquisition closed for up to $50 million. Lower 900 MHz propagation characteristics make these licenses uniquely suited to indoor penetration and wide-area coverage at power levels that can compete with — and in many threat environments, survive — the jamming and spoofing attacks that routinely degrade satellite GPS.

The second pillar is demonstrated technology. In October 2025, NextNav announced the simultaneous delivery of accurate timing and positioning data alongside standard 5G uplink and downlink traffic on commercial 5G network equipment — the critical proof-of-concept for the NextGen platform, which embeds PNT capability into existing 5G base stations using 5G Positioning Reference Signals broadcast on NextNav's licensed spectrum. The demonstration answered the foundational engineering question: the physics works, the waveforms coexist, and the integration path into carrier infrastructure is real.

The third pillar is regulatory momentum. In April 2024, NextNav filed a Petition for Rulemaking asking the FCC to reconfigure the lower 900 MHz band into a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use license enabling 5G NR operations==, structured as a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz paired with a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz==. The FCC responded in March 2025 with a Notice of Inquiry under WT Docket No. 25-110. By early 2026, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking had been noticed to the Office of Management and Budget — the procedural step that precedes formal publication and public comment. The machinery of spectrum policy is moving. Whether it moves fast enough is the operative question.

## Mariam Sorond and the Navigation of Policy

The person tasked with steering NextNav through this process is Mariam Sorond, who serves simultaneously as Chief Executive Officer and Board Chair — a concentration of authority that reflects both the company's scale and the singular focus of its near-term agenda. Sorond's résumé reads like a curriculum vitae assembled specifically for this moment: nearly 30 years across VMware's telco and cloud service provider division, CableLabs — the cable industry's principal R&D and standards body — and DISH Network, where she worked on spectrum deployment strategy. She has served in advisory roles for the NTIA and the FCC, and sits on the CTIA Board of Directors. In an industry where spectrum policy is won or lost at the intersection of technical argumentation and Washington relationships, her background is not incidental. It is the company's primary soft asset.

## The Binary

The thesis is genuinely binary in a way that distinguishes NextNav from almost every other company in the small-cap technology universe. If the FCC approves spectrum reconfiguration under WT Docket No. 25-110, NextNav's ~~12 MHz of licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum~~ ==lower 900 MHz spectrum position — the contiguous 8 MHz over more than 90 percent of the population, augmented by the 4 MHz complementary block —== becomes the licensed backbone of a national GPS resilience mandate — a piece of infrastructure the U.S. government has repeatedly identified as a critical gap, most formally in White House Space Policy Directive 7. The monetization path is carrier licensing: mobile network operators integrate NextGen PNT into their 5G infrastructure, paying NextNav for access to spectrum and technology that turns their existing base stations into a jamming-resistant positioning layer.

If the FCC does not act, or if the rulemaking process extends past June 2028 — when $190 million in 5% senior secured convertible notes mature at a conversion price of $12.56 per share — the commercial model faces severe stress. Cash and short-term investments stood at approximately $152 million as of December 31, 2025, providing an estimated 18 to 24 months of operating runway. The clock and the docket are running in parallel.

## Early Commercial Signals

The forward-looking picture carries two meaningful data points. In December 2025, NextNav signed a technology licensing agreement with MetCom International of Tokyo, the company's first international deal, covering deployment of the NextGen 5G PNT waveform across Japan's largest metropolitan areas pending Japanese regulatory approval. The same month, the October 2025 extension of the AT&T Pinnacle agreement through October 2028 secured the company's primary revenue stream — roughly $4–5 million annually — against near-term attrition. Both events validate commercial demand for the underlying technology.

What they do not provide, as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, is a domestic mobile network operator licensing agreement. No U.S. carrier beyond AT&T's Pinnacle contract has announced an integration with NextNav's NextGen platform. The gap between international proof-of-concept licensing and domestic carrier adoption is precisely where the spectrum reconfiguration decision matters most — and where NextNav's $2 billion valuation premium over its revenue base either finds its justification or its reckoning.

chapters.title: From CommLabs to Critical Infrastructure: NextNav's Founding, SPAC Listing, and Spectrum Accumulation, 2007–2025
chapters.body:
## CommLabs, Sunnyvale, 2007

The company that would eventually seek to redesign America's positioning infrastructure began in a Sunnyvale office under a name few people ever knew. CommLabs, incorporated in 2007, was the creation of a small team with backgrounds in wireless systems, GNSS chipsets, and public-safety communications — among them Ganesh M. Pattabiraman, who would serve as chief executive through much of the pre-IPO era, and Dr. Arun Raghupathy, who remained at the company through the frozen snapshot date as Senior Vice President of Technology Development and Chief Technology Officer. Their founding thesis was narrow and specific: GPS satellite signals, attenuating as they passed through steel and concrete, could not reliably locate a caller inside a building or at the base of a glass canyon. For emergency dispatchers responding to 911 calls, that failure was not a product gap — it was a life-safety deficiency that the Federal Communications Commission had already signaled it intended to mandate away.

The FCC's Enhanced 911 rules, and specifically their evolving requirements around z-axis (altitude) accuracy for wireless callers, represented a regulatory pipeline that the CommLabs founders believed would eventually compel carriers to deploy a terrestrial complement to GPS. The core insight was that licensed radio spectrum in the lower 900 MHz band — signals that penetrate structures where satellite signals cannot — could form the backbone of a ground-based positioning network capable of delivering three-dimensional location data at the accuracy levels the FCC would require. The company rebranded as NextNav and set about demonstrating that thesis to both regulators and prospective investors. An early technology demonstration was conducted within the FCC's Communications Security, Reliability and Interoperability Council (CSRIC III) testbed in San Francisco in 2012, providing one of the first third-party reference points for the technology's practical performance.

## Eighteen Years of Private Capital

What followed was an unusually long private-company trajectory — a function less of any strategic preference for staying private than of the fundamental difficulty of commercializing a technology whose addressable market was, at every stage, contingent on regulatory outcomes that remained uncertain. NextNav raised approximately $270 to $284 million in pre-IPO venture capital across multiple rounds from a group of investors that included Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, New Enterprise Associates, Fortress Investment Group, and Oak Investment Partners. The identity of the investors is itself notable: Fortress, a credit and real estate-oriented alternative asset manager, later returned as a lead participant in NextNav's 2025 convertible note financing — suggesting a sophisticated, long-duration view of the spectrum asset's value that differed meaningfully from conventional venture timelines.

The extended private period signaled what patient observers of regulatory-dependent technology commercialization would recognize: building a network that requires both spectrum licensing and carrier integration, in an environment where FCC mandate timelines shift across administrations, does not compress into a standard seven-year venture cycle. By the time NextNav reached its public offering, the company had spent fourteen years and the better part of three hundred million dollars reaching a position where its Pinnacle E911 service was generating meaningful, if modest, commercial revenue.

## The Spartacus SPAC and the Public Market Wager

NextNav merged with Spartacus Acquisition Corporation, a special-purpose acquisition company, completing its Nasdaq listing in October 2021 under the ticker symbol NN. The transaction valued NextNav at approximately $1 billion on a pro-forma basis and raised additional capital intended to fund network expansion, spectrum strategy, and the development of the next-generation TerraPoiNT platform. The goals articulated at listing were ambitious: accelerate Pinnacle deployment, advance TerraPoiNT's commercial readiness, and build the regulatory foundation for a nationwide terrestrial GPS-complement network.

Assessed in hindsight from May 2026, the execution against those listing-time aspirations was partial at best. Pinnacle deployment did advance, eventually covering more than 4,400 U.S. cities and over 90 percent of commercial buildings taller than three stories. But the TerraPoiNT commercial pathway proved substantially more complex than the SPAC narrative implied, and the company's revenue trajectory — declining to $4.6 million in FY 2025, down 19 percent year-over-year — bore little resemblance to the growth curve investors in a SPAC transaction might have expected. The stock, listed into a market that was broadly generous to infrastructure and deep-technology concepts in late 2021, subsequently experienced the same multiple compression that punished most pre-revenue SPAC graduates as rates rose and patience for long-duration regulatory bets thinned.

## Nestwave: Buying the Receiver

The most consequential acquisition in NextNav's post-IPO history closed in November 2022. NextNav acquired Nestwave SAS, a Neuilly-sur-Seine, France-based developer of LTE and 5G receiver signal-processing technology, for approximately $18 million — structured as roughly $4.3 million in cash and $13 million to $15 million in NextNav stock.

The strategic rationale was direct: Nestwave's receiver technology allowed TerraPoiNT-compatible positioning signals to be extracted from existing cellular network signals rather than requiring specialized, purpose-built hardware in end-user devices. The company estimated the acquisition could reduce deployment costs by approximately 75 percent — a figure that addressed one of the principal commercial objections to TerraPoiNT as a standalone overlay network, which was that requiring new chipsets or dedicated hardware across hundreds of millions of devices made adoption economics prohibitive for carriers. By embedding the positioning capability into the 5G signal processing stack, NextNav could approach mobile network operators with a software and spectrum solution rather than a hardware deployment program. The Nestwave team, retained as the core of a Paris-area engineering function, became the technical foundation of what NextNav would later brand the NextGen platform.

## The Spectrum Accumulation and the April 2024 Petition

NextNav's original spectrum position consisted of Mobile Location and Monitoring Service (M-LMS) licenses in the 902–928 MHz band — a band whose regulatory history was itself complex, reflecting earlier iterations of location services licensing that predated the modern GPS-complement framing. The company's spectrum strategy through the early 2020s focused on consolidating holdings and building the operational and technical record that would support a petition for structural band reconfiguration.

That petition arrived in April 2024: a formal Petition for Rulemaking filed with the FCC requesting reconfiguration of the lower 900 MHz band to create a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use license enabling 5G NR-based terrestrial PNT operations. ==The proposed structure was a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz paired with a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz.== The accompanying economic analysis, conducted by The Brattle Group, estimated the proposal would deliver $14.6 billion in total economic value, including $10.8 billion in what the study characterized as GPS outage insurance value. In September 2025, NextNav closed an acquisition of additional lower 900 MHz band licenses — announced earlier in 2024 for up to $50 million in total consideration — bringing its total holdings to ~~12 MHz of contiguous spectrum covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population~~ ==12 MHz of lower 900 MHz spectrum: an 8 MHz contiguous block covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population, complemented by an additional 4 MHz covering part of the U.S. population==.

The spectrum buildout ran in parallel with the commercial deployment of Pinnacle. In one sense, the Pinnacle network served dual purposes: it generated the AT&T FirstNet revenue that provided NextNav its only substantial commercial cash flow, and it demonstrated to regulators and prospective carrier partners that NextNav could build, operate, and maintain a nationwide low-band radio infrastructure. The FCC received NextNav's petition against this operational backdrop.

## Eighteen Years and Five Hundred Million Dollars

By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, NextNav had spent approximately eighteen years and, by a rough accounting that combines pre-IPO venture capital with post-SPAC operating losses and acquisition outlays, something in the vicinity of five hundred million dollars reaching a singular strategic position: the company held ~~12 MHz of licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum covering nearly the entire U.S. population~~ ==12 MHz of licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum — an 8 MHz contiguous block reaching more than 90 percent of the U.S. population, plus 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the population==, operated a proven E911 altitude network across thousands of cities, had demonstrated 5G-native simultaneous positioning and data transmission on commercial equipment, and had filed — and was awaiting action on — the FCC rulemaking petition that would determine whether any of it could scale.

The historiographical reading of that arc is not straightforward. The founding team identified a genuine gap and a genuine regulatory lever early — a display of original insight. The private investors, including Fortress, took a long-duration view that ultimately positioned the company well for the spectrum strategy pivot. The Nestwave acquisition, small in price but large in strategic implication, showed the kind of precise capital deployment that a resource-constrained company in a regulatory holding pattern needed to execute. Against those credits, the SPAC transaction delivered capital but also imposed a public-market reporting structure on a company whose value was inherently binary and whose commercial timeline was measured in regulatory cycles rather than fiscal quarters. The result, by May 2026, was a company whose equity market capitalization exceeded $2 billion on revenues of $4.6 million — a valuation sustained entirely by the market's assignment of probability to a single regulatory outcome. Whether the eighteen-year arc represented visionary persistence or a slow-motion test of investor patience remained, at the frozen snapshot date, genuinely unresolved.

chapters.title: Pinnacle, TerraPoiNT, and NextGen: NextNav's Three-Platform Architecture for Terrestrial PNT
chapters.body:
## The Problem That Spectrum Solves

The Global Positioning System's fundamental limitation is geometric. Its 31 operational satellites orbit roughly 20,200 kilometres above the Earth's surface, transmitting signals at power levels so attenuated by the time they reach the ground — approximately -130 dBm at the receiver — that any substantial obstruction renders them unreliable or unusable. That vulnerability manifests in three distinct failure modes, each of which shaped a different corner of NextNav's product architecture.

Inside commercial buildings, reinforced concrete, steel framing, and the compounding attenuation of multiple floor slabs reduce GPS signal strength to the point where receivers either lose lock entirely or produce position estimates with vertical errors measured in dozens of metres. For a 911 dispatcher trying to locate a cardiac patient collapsed on the fourteenth floor of a Chicago office tower, a horizontal position accurate to ten metres means nothing if the vertical coordinate is wrong by eight floors. Urban canyons create a second failure mode through multipath: satellite signals reflecting off glass and steel facades arrive at the receiver via multiple paths with different travel times, distorting both position and timing estimates in ways that are difficult to model and impossible to eliminate with antenna design alone. The third failure mode is deliberate. GPS operates on a civilian signal broadcast at a known frequency with publicly documented structure — a design choice made in the 1970s that makes the system trivially jammable with equipment costing hundreds of dollars and spoofable with software-defined radio hardware available commercially. The proliferation of GPS jamming incidents around military bases, ports, and conflict zones in Eastern Europe and the Middle East made clear during the 2020s that satellite-only PNT represented a critical national infrastructure vulnerability, not merely a consumer inconvenience.

NextNav's three platforms — Pinnacle, TerraPoiNT, and the NextGen 5G system — each address one or more of these failure modes using a common foundation: licensed radio spectrum in the lower 900 MHz band, broadcast from terrestrial infrastructure at power levels orders of magnitude above GPS.

## Pinnacle: The Floor-Level E911 Foundation

Pinnacle is NextNav's oldest and only revenue-generating service. It operates on a deceptively simple physical insight: barometric pressure varies predictably with altitude, and a smartphone's onboard pressure sensor, when calibrated against a known reference measured at the same time and nearby location, can determine floor level with sufficient accuracy to satisfy emergency dispatch requirements.

The calibration network is the defensible asset. NextNav installed barometric reference pressure sensors in commercial buildings across more than 4,400 U.S. cities, achieving coverage of over 90 percent of commercial buildings taller than three stories. When a 911 call is placed from a multi-storey building, the smartphone's pressure reading is compared in real time against NextNav's nearest calibrated reference point, yielding a vertical position estimate accurate to approximately three metres — sufficient to identify floor level in standard commercial construction. The FCC's z-axis location accuracy mandates, adopted under the Wireless E911 Location Accuracy Requirements framework, created the regulatory demand that justified building this infrastructure. The mandates require wireless carriers to provide dispatchable location — including floor level — for a substantial percentage of indoor 911 calls, and Pinnacle was designed specifically to meet that standard.

The commercial delivery mechanism runs through AT&T's FirstNet public-safety broadband network. Under a multi-year operations agreement, AT&T embeds Pinnacle's floor-level data into the location payload of 911 calls routed over FirstNet — the dedicated public-safety LTE network built under the 2012 Middle Class Tax Relief Act. In October 2025, NextNav extended that agreement by two years through October 2028, securing what had by that point become approximately 89 percent of quarterly revenue. The extension validated the service's operational relevance to the FirstNet ecosystem but simultaneously underscored the customer concentration risk that pervades NextNav's income statement.

Pinnacle's ceiling as a business, however, is clearly visible. The E911 mandate creates a durable revenue floor, not a growth engine. The service does not scale with 5G deployment cycles, does not attract new carrier customers easily, and generates revenue in the low single-digit millions annually against a company burning tens of millions of dollars per quarter. Its strategic value to NextNav is operational — it maintains an engineering team, a nationwide sensor network, and a carrier relationship — rather than financial.

## TerraPoiNT: Ground-Based GPS Analog

TerraPoiNT represents NextNav's technological ambition at its most direct. The system is, in architectural terms, a terrestrial reimplementation of GPS: a network of synchronized ground-based transmitters broadcasting positioning signals at known locations, allowing receivers to calculate three-dimensional position through time-of-arrival measurements across multiple transmitters.

The critical difference from GPS is power. TerraPoiNT transmitters operate on NextNav's licensed 920–928 MHz spectrum at signal strengths approximately 10,000 times greater than GPS satellite signals received at ground level. That power advantage is not incidental — it is the system's principal selling proposition. Signals that strong penetrate building structures, propagate through urban canyons without the multipath fragility of satellite geometry, and are extraordinarily difficult to jam without also disrupting the entire 900 MHz band across a large geographic area. For national security applications — protecting aviation navigation, port timing systems, military base operations — the jamming resistance of a high-power terrestrial signal operating on licensed domestic spectrum represents a qualitatively different resilience profile than GPS augmentation systems that remain dependent on the same vulnerable satellite downlink.

TerraPoiNT's precision credentials were established by independent federal evaluation. In 2021, the U.S. Department of Transportation conducted comparative testing of alternative PNT solutions as part of the federal government's post-Space Policy Directive 7 effort to identify credible GPS complements. TerraPoiNT ranked highest among all evaluated alternative systems across the assessment's evaluation metrics — a result NextNav has cited consistently in regulatory filings and investor communications as evidence of government-validated technical performance. Timing synchronization testing demonstrated accuracy better than 50 nanoseconds, a benchmark relevant for the telecommunications synchronisation applications — 5G base station timing, financial transaction timestamping, power grid coordination — where GPS provides critical infrastructure timing rather than navigation.

As of the frozen snapshot, TerraPoiNT networks were operational in two markets: the San Francisco Bay Area and McLean, Virginia, the latter a location whose proximity to federal national-security infrastructure is unlikely to be coincidental. Neither deployment had produced material commercial revenue. TerraPoiNT's commercialisation path always faced the same structural problem: building a standalone overlay network of synchronized transmitters nationwide would require capital expenditure comparable to a small wireless carrier build-out — feasible only with government anchor contracts or carrier partnerships that had not materialised at scale.

## NextGen: PNT Embedded in 5G Infrastructure

The NextGen platform is NextNav's answer to TerraPoiNT's deployment cost problem, and it represents the company's primary long-term commercial thesis. The core insight is that 5G New Radio already incorporates a positioning reference signal framework — 5G Positioning Reference Signals (PRS) — standardised within the 3GPP specification to enable sub-metre indoor positioning for 5G networks. NextNav's approach is to repurpose that framework to broadcast TerraPoiNT-grade terrestrial PNT signals through standard commercial 5G base station hardware using NextNav's licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum as the transmission medium.

If the architecture works at commercial scale, the economics invert. Instead of NextNav building its own transmitter network, mobile network operators would integrate NextNav's PNT capability into their existing 5G infrastructure, with NextNav licensing the waveform and receiver technology and potentially collecting per-device or per-transmission fees. The capital burden shifts to carriers who are already deploying 5G base stations; NextNav's licensed spectrum becomes the input that enables a GPS-complement capability those carriers cannot otherwise offer on their own.

The Nestwave acquisition, completed in November 2022, was essential to closing the receiver-side of this architecture. Nestwave, a Neuilly-sur-Seine-based startup, had developed low-power 5G PRS receiver technology capable of extracting positioning information from 5G signals on standard handset hardware. Without a capable receiver, the transmitter network is commercially inert. With Nestwave's technology integrated into the NextGen platform, NextNav could credibly claim a complete system — transmit on licensed spectrum, receive on commercial 5G devices — rather than a half-built infrastructure in search of a chipset partner.

The October 2025 proof-of-concept demonstration confirmed the core technical claim: NextNav successfully delivered simultaneous accurate timing and positioning data alongside standard 5G uplink and downlink traffic on commercial 5G network equipment. The demonstration validated that PNT and data services are not mutually exclusive on the same carrier infrastructure — a key objection that had been raised about spectrum efficiency trade-offs. A commercial-scale demonstration targeting Santa Clara County was planned for late 2025, representing the transition from controlled lab conditions to a real-world multi-site deployment.

## The Spectrum Architecture Underneath Everything

All three platforms share a common dependency: NextNav's licensed holdings in the 902–928 MHz Mobile Location and Monitoring Service band. The lower 900 MHz range was selected for its propagation characteristics — longer wavelengths penetrate building materials more effectively than the higher-frequency bands used by most 5G deployments, and the band's geographic coverage economics favour wide-area terrestrial network construction.

As of September 2025, following the close of a licence acquisition announced in 2024 for up to $50 million, NextNav held ~~12 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population, expanded from 8 MHz~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population, plus an additional 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the U.S. population==. The current band plan, however, does not accommodate 5G NR operations in its native form. The 902–928 MHz band is currently allocated for non-exclusive unlicensed use alongside NextNav's licensed M-LMS assignments, creating an interference environment incompatible with the carrier-grade reliability 5G service requires.

NextNav's April 2024 FCC Petition for Rulemaking proposed to resolve this through a fundamental band reconfiguration: creating a 5 MHz ~~paired ~~uplink at 902–907 MHz ==and== a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz~~, and an additional 5 MHz for supplemental services~~ — yielding a 15 MHz flexible-use licence enabling 5G NR operations under Part 27 rules. Without that reconfiguration, NextGen remains technically demonstrated but commercially stranded. The FCC's March 2025 Notice of Inquiry in WT Docket No. 25-110 and the subsequent OMB notification of a pending Notice of Proposed Rulemaking represented the regulatory process advancing toward the decision on which the entire NextGen commercial thesis rests.

## MetCom and the Proof-of-Concept Frontier

In December 2025, NextNav signed a strategic technology licensing agreement with MetCom International of Tokyo — the company's first international commercial licence. MetCom licensed NextNav's 5G-based 3D PNT waveform and receiver technologies for deployment across Japan's largest metropolitan areas, subject to Japanese regulatory approval. The agreement confirmed international demand for the NextGen architecture and demonstrated that a credible technology partner in a sophisticated wireless market had evaluated the system and concluded it merited investment in licensing rights.

The MetCom agreement was, however, a licensing transaction at proof-of-concept scale, not a commercial deployment at mobile network operator scale. Japan's 5G PNT regulatory framework had not been finalised, MetCom's deployment timeline remained subject to that approval process, and no equivalent domestic U.S. carrier licensing agreement existed outside the existing AT&T Pinnacle contract. The gap between validated technology and operational nationwide 5G PNT infrastructure — across hundreds of thousands of base stations, integrated into carrier network management systems, delivered to hundreds of millions of devices — was the distance NextNav's balance sheet and regulatory strategy would need to close before the June 2028 maturity of its $190 million convertible war chest.

chapters.title: Microscopic Revenue, Maximum Losses: NextNav's Capital Structure, Burn Rate, and the Convertible Note Clock
chapters.body:
## The Defining Arithmetic

No financial fact about NextNav Inc. is more disorienting than the gap between what the company earns and what the market says it is worth. In the twelve months ended December 31, 2025, NextNav recorded $4.6 million in revenue. At the same time, with its shares trading at roughly $22 to $23 on Nasdaq as of May 2026, the company carried a market capitalisation ~~exceeding $2.2 billion~~ ==of approximately $3.0 billion against 135.6 million common shares outstanding as of March 13, 2026==. The implied price-to-sales ratio — somewhere above ~~350~~ ==660== times trailing revenue — placed NextNav beyond the taxonomy of conventional technology valuation. This was not a growth stock trading at a premium to current earnings; it was an entity whose market price bore essentially no relationship to its income statement. What the equity market was pricing, with uncomfortable precision, was not NextNav's current business but its regulatory future: specifically, the probability and magnitude of an FCC spectrum reconfiguration that would transform 12 megahertz of licensed lower 900 MHz radio spectrum into the foundation of a national 5G positioning, navigation, and timing backbone.

That valuation logic is internally consistent. It is also acutely vulnerable to regulatory delay, reversal, or competitive displacement — and it is sustained, in the interim, by a capital structure whose clock is now audibly ticking.

## Revenue Architecture: Growth, Contraction, and the 89 Percent Problem

NextNav's commercial revenue history is brief and instructive. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2023, the company reported [$3.9 million in total revenue](https://ir.nextnav.com/financial-information/sec-filings), derived almost entirely from the Pinnacle E911 floor-level altitude service delivered through its operations agreement with AT&T's FirstNet public-safety broadband network. Fiscal 2024 produced apparent momentum: revenue rose 46 percent year-over-year to $5.7 million, reflecting milestone payments and service fee step-ups embedded in the AT&T contract structure rather than new commercial relationships.

The 2025 reversal was more telling. Full-year FY 2025 revenue fell to $4.6 million, a 19 percent year-over-year decline, as the timing of contract milestone recognition shifted and no new revenue streams materialised to compensate. Quarterly granularity exposed the structural fragility of the revenue base. In the three months ended September 30, 2025, NextNav recorded just $887,000 in revenue — a 44.8 percent decline from the prior-year quarter — and a single customer accounted for 89 percent of that figure. ==The Q1 2026 print, released ahead of the snapshot date, extended that pattern: $995,000 in revenue against a $10.6 million net loss, with no new material customers disclosed.== The identity of that customer was not in doubt: AT&T and FirstNet have constituted the near-totality of NextNav's commercial income since the Pinnacle service launched.

|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | $3.9 million | — |
| FY 2024 | $5.7 million | +46% |
| FY 2025 | $4.6 million | −19% |
| Q3 2025 (single quarter) | $0.9 million | −44.8% |
| ==Q1 2026 (single quarter)== | ==$1.0 million== | ==n/m== |

The concentration risk is not merely an investor relations talking point. It represents an operational reality: NextNav's revenue function effectively has one variable, which is the pace and structure of payments from a single counterparty under a contract extended through October 2028. The November 2023 federal agency contract for GPS characterisation services and the December 2025 MetCom International licensing agreement in Japan each represent potential diversification, but neither had produced material revenue within the frozen snapshot period.

## Operating Losses, Net Losses, and the Non-Cash Divergence

Beneath the revenue line, NextNav maintained a broadly stable operating cost structure across the three-year period, though "stable" in this context means persistently and substantially loss-generating. The company recorded operating losses of $63.5 million in FY 2023, $60.1 million in FY 2024, and $70.2 million in FY 2025. The FY 2025 increase reflected elevated R&D expenditure on the NextGen 5G platform — including the integration of technology from the Nestwave SAS acquisition in Neuilly-sur-Seine — and the considerable legal and regulatory advocacy costs associated with advancing FCC WT Docket No. 25-110 through its procedural stages.

The divergence between operating and net losses, however, is where the income statement becomes genuinely complex. Net losses were $71.7 million in FY 2023, $101.9 million in FY 2024, and $189.3 million in FY 2025. The escalating gap between operating and net loss figures — approximately $8 million in FY 2023, $41.8 million in FY 2024 (including $32.2 million in warrant-related charges), and $119.1 million in FY 2025 — does not reflect a deterioration in the underlying business's cost structure. It reflects, instead, the accounting treatment of NextNav's successive debt financing transactions: warrant liability remeasurement, derivative fair value adjustments on the convertible notes, and the one-time debt extinguishment charges recognised when the March 2025 refinancing redeemed the prior senior secured notes. These are non-cash charges with no operational content, but they produce headline net loss figures of a magnitude that would trigger alarm in any business where revenue could plausibly service the losses. In NextNav's case, the operating loss itself tells the more relevant story: a company burning approximately $60 to $70 million annually against a revenue base of $4 to $6 million. ==The Q1 2026 net loss of $10.6 million was substantially smaller than the recent quarterly cadence, reflecting favourable derivative remeasurement rather than a step-change in operating burn.==

## The March 2025 Refinancing: Structure and Accounting Consequences

The most consequential transaction in NextNav's financial history occurred on March 27, 2025, when the company closed a [$190 million senior secured convertible note financing](https://ir.nextnav.com/financial-information/sec-filings) that fundamentally restructured its capital position. The notes carry a 5 percent annual coupon — half the rate of the prior 10 percent Senior Secured Notes they replaced — and mature in June 2028, with a conversion price of $12.56 per share. The lead investors were Fortress Investment Group affiliates, already significant shareholders and the company's prior secured lender, and M-Cor Capital, the investment vehicle of the Milken Family Office.

Net proceeds were approximately $188.6 million. A portion of those proceeds redeemed the outstanding $70 million of 10 percent Senior Secured Notes at 101 percent of par — a modest premium that reflected both the lender's consent requirement and the company's incentive to eliminate the near-term 2026 maturity. The effective economic benefit of the refinancing was threefold: it extended the debt maturity by more than two years, it halved the cash interest burden (from roughly $7 million annually on the prior notes to approximately $9.5 million on the new, larger face value), and it provided a net cash infusion that, post-redemption, materially extended the operating runway.

The accounting consequences were more complicated. Under GAAP treatment applicable to convertible instruments with embedded derivatives, NextNav was required to recognise a derivative liability associated with the conversion feature and certain redemption rights, creating an unamortized discount on the notes and bifurcating the instrument between debt and derivative components. As of December 31, 2025, the balance sheet reflected long-term debt of $273.6 million — substantially in excess of the $190 million face value — as a consequence of the derivative fair value adjustments accreted into the carrying amount. This accounting treatment, combined with accumulated net losses, produced negative book equity: the company's total stockholders' deficit as of year-end 2025 was material, notwithstanding the underlying economic improvement represented by the refinancing. ==The convertible's 15.127 million underlying shares were excluded from diluted EPS as anti-dilutive in the FY 2025 filings, but they sit on the share-count horizon as a structural overhang that would, on conversion at $12.56, expand the diluted base to roughly 150.7 million shares.==

## Liquidity Runway and the 2028 Clock

Cash management is the governing operational constraint for a company burning $60 to $70 million per year against minimal revenue. As of December 31, 2024, NextNav held $80.1 million in liquid assets — sufficient for slightly over twelve months of operating cash consumption at historical rates, creating a meaningful refinancing urgency that the March 2025 transaction directly addressed. Post-financing, the September 30, 2025 balance sheet reflected $167.6 million in cash and short-term investments, declining to approximately $152 million by December 31, 2025, as the company returned to its baseline burn cadence.

The implied quarterly cash consumption rate — roughly $15 to $16 million, consistent with a $60 to $65 million annualised operating cash outflow — suggests the December 2025 cash position provides approximately 9 to 10 quarters of runway before reaching a level that would trigger going-concern disclosure thresholds. Management guided, in its FY 2025 filings, that the current position funds operations beyond twelve months from the reporting date, which is a standard but meaningful disclosure. The more precise analytical question is when the liquidity position falls below a twelve-month threshold relative to the June 2028 debt maturity — a date that concentrates attention on the FCC rulemaking calendar in a way that management presentations rarely articulate directly.

## The Spectrum Asset GAAP Cannot Price

Against $273.6 million in balance-sheet debt and negative book equity, NextNav carried spectrum licenses valued at approximately $33 million on its balance sheet as of the frozen snapshot date. This figure represents the historical cost of the company's M-LMS licenses in the 902–928 MHz band — ~~a 12 MHz nationwide holding covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population~~ ==a 12 MHz aggregate holding in which 8 MHz forms a contiguous near-nationwide block covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population and the additional 4 MHz is complementary spectrum covering a partial-population footprint==, assembled over eighteen years through original grants and the September 2025 acquisition of additional licenses for up to $50 million in total consideration.

The $33 million carrying value is, in one sense, an accounting artefact. GAAP requires spectrum licenses to be carried at historical cost less impairment; it has no mechanism for recognising the regulatory optionality embedded in a license that may, subject to FCC approval, be reconfigured into a 15 MHz flexible-use nationwide 5G allocation ==— specifically, a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz paired with a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz, as set out in the FCC petition==. The implied market value of those spectrum rights, as embedded in NextNav's equity capitalisation, is many hundreds of millions of dollars by any residual-value analysis. The Brattle Group, in the economic study commissioned to support the FCC petition, attributed $10.8 billion in GPS outage insurance value alone to the proposed reconfiguration — a figure that, if partially capitalised into a licensing royalty stream, would transform the spectrum asset from a $33 million line item into a franchise worth multiples of the company's current market capitalisation.

## A Levered Call Option on the FCC Outcome

At $22 to $23 per share in May 2026, against a 52-week range of $10.84 to $24.19, NextNav's equity traded at a level that admitted only one coherent interpretation: the market was pricing the shares as a levered call option on the FCC spectrum reconfiguration outcome, with the $190 million convertible note serving as both the instrument of leverage and the source of the expiry pressure.

A simplified probability-weighted framework illustrates the logic. If the FCC approves the spectrum reconfiguration and NextNav successfully licenses the NextGen platform to U.S. carriers and international operators, a reasonable bull-case intrinsic value might place per-share value in the $40 to $60 range, assuming a mid-single-digit royalty on a fraction of the U.S. 5G infrastructure market. If the rulemaking fails or is indefinitely deferred, NextNav's intrinsic value reverts to the liquidation value of its spectrum licenses, its Pinnacle cash flows discounted through 2028, and the residual cash position net of debt — a figure that, given the convertible note overhang, likely approaches zero for equity holders. Applying a binary probability model at a current share price of roughly $22.50, the implied market probability of the favourable outcome sits somewhere between ~~35~~ ==38== and ~~50~~ ==56== percent, depending on the assumed success-case valuation and the discount rate applied to the optionality.

That range is neither obviously right nor obviously wrong. It captures, with appropriate imprecision, what the financial structure of NextNav actually is: a company spending $65 million a year to hold its position in a regulatory proceeding whose outcome, when it comes, will determine whether the convertible note is refinanced into a scaled commercial enterprise or whether the clock simply runs out.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Spectrum-Optionality Premium

NextNav's equity cannot be valued with conventional financial tools. The trailing twelve-month revenue figure — $4.6 million for fiscal year 2025, or roughly the quarterly intake of a modestly busy car wash — is incidental to what the market is actually pricing. Price-to-earnings, EV/EBITDA, and price-to-book are not merely unhelpful here; they are arithmetically unavailable. The company has never earned a profit. Its EBITDA runs at a loss approaching $70 million annually. The March 2025 convertible-note financing created negative book equity through derivative liability accounting. What remains is a single operative multiple: price-to-revenue, currently in the range of ~~480–510x~~ ==640–680x== on a ~~$2.2–$2.5 billion~~ ==$2.95–3.25 billion== market capitalization against fiscal 2025 revenue of $4.6 million, and an enterprise value — market cap plus $190 million in face-value debt, less approximately $152 million in cash — of roughly ~~$2.4 billion, implying an EV-to-revenue ratio exceeding 500x~~ ==$3.0 billion, implying an EV-to-revenue ratio around 650x==.

Those numbers are not a valuation in the conventional sense. They are a probability. The market is not pricing NextNav's current business. It is pricing the outcome of FCC WT Docket No. 25-110 and the petition to reconfigure ~~12 MHz of licensed lower-900 MHz spectrum into a nationwide 5G-compatible PNT infrastructure backbone~~ ==NextNav's lower-900 MHz holdings — 8 MHz of contiguous spectrum covering more than 90% of the U.S. population plus 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the country — into a 15 MHz nationwide 5G-compatible PNT channelization, specifically a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz and a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz==.

## Where Conventional Metrics Break Down: A Peer Comparison

Direct peers do not exist. No other publicly traded U.S. company holds a comparable licensed-spectrum position with an equivalent FCC rulemaking pending. The peer group below is built from partial analogues — companies sharing one or two key attributes with NextNav but not the full profile. The resulting table is illustrative rather than definitive; peer multiples are approximate as of the frozen window.

| Company | Ticker | Profile | EV / Revenue | EV / EBITDA | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NextNav Inc. | NN | Licensed 900 MHz spectrum; pre-commercial; GPS-backup infrastructure | ~~520x~~ ==~650x== | N/M (neg.) | FY2025 rev. $4.6M; market cap ~~$2.2–2.5B~~ ==~$3.0B== |
| Anterix Inc. | ATEX | Licensed 900 MHz spectrum for private LTE; regulatory-optionality model | ~30–60x | N/M (neg.) | Minimal revenue from spectrum leases; no active NPRM equivalent |
| Iridium Communications | IRDM | Satellite-based PNT timing and data services; global network | ~6–8x | ~14–17x | Profitable; ~$900M TTM revenue; established commercial base |
| Trimble Inc. | TRMB | GNSS/PNT hardware and software; enterprise positioning | ~3–5x | ~18–22x | Diversified, profitable; $3.5–4B revenue; no spectrum optionality |
| Comtech Telecommunications | CMTL | Government GPS augmentation; satellite communications | ~1–2x | N/M | Revenue declining; financially stressed; limited comparability |
| Ondas Holdings | ONDS | Small-cap wireless infrastructure; defense and industrial IoT | ~8–15x | N/M (neg.) | Pre-profitability; government contract dependency |

*Peer figures approximate; for illustrative comparison only. NextNav multiples calculated from [SEC EDGAR filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001865631&type=10-K).*

The gap between NextNav's EV/revenue multiple and Anterix's — the closest structural analog, sharing the same licensed 900 MHz band and a regulatory-optionality thesis — is itself the clearest expression of what the market is pricing. Anterix trades at a premium to revenue reflecting its spectrum position, but at an order of magnitude lower than NextNav. The difference is the FCC rulemaking: NextNav has an active NPRM progression in WT Docket No. 25-110, advanced far enough for the OMB to have received notification of the pending proposed rule. Anterix has no equivalent catalyst. What NextNav's multiple captures, that no peer replicates, is the binary upside of a favorable Final Rule arriving before a fixed debt maturity.

## Historical Trajectory: A Ratchet, Not a Range

NextNav debuted on Nasdaq via its SPAC merger with Spartacus Acquisition Corporation in October 2021, listing near $10 per share before the first wave of SPAC-era deflation. Through 2022 and 2023, as rising interest rates compressed small-cap speculative equities broadly, the stock traded between roughly $3 and $8 — a de-rating that reflected the modest pace of FCC progress and the absence of a visible near-term commercial catalyst for the NextGen platform.

The re-rating began in earnest in 2024, when the April 2024 Petition for Rulemaking was filed and the stock began attracting a dedicated audience of spectrum-policy investors. Each regulatory milestone since — the FCC's March 2025 Notice of Inquiry, the OMB NPRM notification in early 2026, the December 2025 MetCom international licensing deal — drove a successive multiple expansion. The 52-week range as of the frozen window, $10.84 to $24.19 per share, captures that arc; the stock's positioning near the upper half of that range reflects a market currently assigning high, though not certain, probability to a favorable FCC outcome.

## What the Market Is Pricing In

The most tractable framework for the current valuation is not a forward earnings model — there are no near-term earnings — but a probability-weighted scenario analysis anchored to the June 2028 debt maturity.

At approximately $22 per share and roughly ~~97 million diluted shares outstanding (including approximately 15 million shares from full conversion of the $190 million convertible note at $12.56 per share)~~ ==135.6 million common shares outstanding as of March 13, 2026 (with the 15.1 million conversion shares from the $190 million 2028 convertible note at $12.56 per share excluded from diluted EPS as anti-dilutive under the company's net-loss accounting)==, the market capitalization is roughly ~~$2.1~~ ==$3.0== billion. Enterprise value is approximately ~~$2.15~~ ==$3.0== billion.

Working backwards: if full FCC approval and carrier-licensing commercialization could support a business worth $6–8 billion by 2029–2030 — roughly 10–12x revenues of $500–600 million in a licensing-at-scale scenario, discounted at 15% — and if a failed or delayed rulemaking leaves the company worth $300–500 million in spectrum-option and cash-remnant value, then the current price of approximately $22 per share implies the market is assigning roughly ~~25–35%~~ ==35–45%== probability to the full-bull outcome, with the remaining probability mass distributed across base and bear cases that still attribute meaningful option value to the spectrum holdings.

Alternatively stated: the current enterprise value of approximately ~~$2.15~~ ==$3.0== billion prices in a roughly ~~35–40%~~ ==45–55%== probability that NextGen achieves commercial licensing revenues approaching $300–400 million within five years — a figure representing 65–85x the company's current annual revenue.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — FCC Final Rule issued by mid-2027, first domestic MNO licensing deal by year-end 2027.** NextNav closes its first U.S. mobile network operator licensing agreement during 2027, converting the FCC approval into contracted revenue. Revenue inflects from the $5 million range toward $50–100 million in licensing and government contracts by 2028, with line-of-sight to $300–500 million by 2030 as additional carriers replicate the MetCom model domestically. The convertible notes are refinanced or repaid at maturity without dilution. At a 15–20x revenue multiple appropriate for a high-growth infrastructure licensor, a $300 million revenue base implies a $4.5–6 billion enterprise value, translating to roughly ~~$40–55~~ ==$33–44== per share on the current diluted share count. **Bull-case implied price: ~~$45–55~~ ==$33–44==.**

**Base case — NPRM issues in 2026, Final Rule takes until 2028 with meaningful interference conditions, commercial traction limited before debt maturity.** The FCC proceeds at its deliberative pace, requiring additional comment periods addressing coexistence concerns from incumbent 900 MHz operators, Apple, and device manufacturers. A Final Rule with guard-band and power-limit conditions emerges in mid-to-late 2028, roughly coincident with the debt maturity. NextNav refinances the convertible notes — likely with some dilution — while securing government-channel revenue and incremental international licensing agreements. Revenue reaches $15–30 million by 2027, sufficient to demonstrate the model but insufficient to drive a step-change in the multiple. The stock consolidates near current levels, bounded below by spectrum-option value and above by unresolved commercial execution risk. **Base-case price range: $17–25.**

**Bear case — FCC delays or conditions spectrum reconfiguration beyond 2028, or imposes interference mitigation that renders the business model uneconomic.** The NPRM, when issued, incorporates interference-protection requirements — driven by the organized opposition coalition of Apple, NTIA, the GPS Innovation Alliance, and incumbent 900 MHz users — stringent enough that the resulting license conditions are inconsistent with a commercially deployable nationwide 5G PNT network. NextNav enters 2028 with its debt maturing, revenues still sub-$10 million, and no domestic carrier commitments. A distressed refinancing, partial asset sale (spectrum licenses, Nestwave SAS), or recapitalization at depressed prices follows. Spectrum-only liquidation value and remaining cash might support ~~$3–5~~ ==$2–4== per share; a dilutive financing to sustain operations could compress realized per-share value toward the lower bound of that range. **Bear-case implied price: ~~$3–7~~ ==$2–5==.**

## The Gap Between Consensus and This Read

The market's current pricing near $21–23 per share reflects the late-stage FCC progression and discounts the bear scenario to a low probability — consistent with the OMB NPRM notification and the bipartisan Congressional momentum around GPS resilience. Where this analysis diverges from the implied consensus is on timeline and conditions risk.

The organized opposition to the rulemaking petition — Apple's interference engineering concerns, NTIA's cautious posture, the GPS Innovation Alliance's incumbent-protection advocacy — has not abated since the April 2024 filing. The FCC's standard practice of issuing a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking does not guarantee a Final Rule favorable to the petitioner; proceedings routinely extend over multiple years and produce outcomes materially narrower than the petition requested. NextNav's June 2028 debt maturity creates a hard deadline that the FCC's deliberative calendar may not accommodate comfortably, and a refinancing under adverse conditions or an unfavorable rule would be significantly dilutive to common equity holders.

At $22 per share, NextNav is not expensive if the spectrum thesis is correct. It is extraordinarily expensive if it is not. The current valuation leaves almost no margin for error in timing, regulatory outcome, or commercial execution — a risk profile that the company's management has acknowledged, implicitly, by securing 18–24 months of liquidity through the March 2025 convertible financing and by framing the FCC NPRM notification as the pivotal marker of institutional validation. The next twelve months, spanning the expected NPRM comment period and the path toward a Final Rule, will determine which scenario the probability mass migrates toward.

chapters.title: Twelve Quarters of Conviction: NextNav's Earnings Call Narrative from 2023 Through Q1 2026
chapters.body:
## Establishing the Thesis, 2023

NextNav entered 2023 as a company with a story that outpaced its financial reality by a considerable margin. Full-year revenue for FY 2023 came in at approximately $3.9 million — a figure that would attract little institutional attention in isolation — against an operating loss of $63.5 million and a net loss of $71.7 million. The asymmetry between income statement and market narrative was already the defining tension of the investment case. On quarterly calls through 2023, management's consistent message positioned the Pinnacle altitude-location service as proof of concept and revenue floor, while TerraPoiNT's terrestrial signal architecture was described as a technically validated GPS complement awaiting only policy enablement to become a national infrastructure asset.

The November 2023 federal agency contract — for GPS and PNT characterization services — provided a concrete data point that management could deploy to support this framing. The contract was never large enough to be material to the income statement, but its signaling value was disproportionate: a named federal agency had evaluated the technology and committed budget, lending credibility to the national-security narrative that would underpin the FCC rulemaking petition. Through 2023, management consistently described the regulatory path as a deliberate, multiyear process in its early stages, using language that was measured and forward-looking without offering specific timing commitments.

## The Petition Year: 2024

The April 2024 filing of the FCC Petition for Rulemaking marked a decisive shift in the earnings narrative. Revenue for FY 2024 reached $5.7 million, a 46 percent increase year-over-year, lending a degree of commercial momentum to the call. For the first time, management had a specific regulatory instrument to reference — not just a general advocacy program, but a formal document requesting reconfiguration of the 902–928 MHz band into ~~a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use 5G NR license~~ ==a 15 MHz 5G NR license structured as a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz paired with a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz==. The Brattle Group's independent economic study, valuing the proposal at $14.6 billion in total economic benefit including $10.8 billion in GPS outage insurance value, gave management a citable third-party figure that reframed the opportunity in infrastructure terms rather than technology terms.

The 2024 calls reflected a more confident regulatory vocabulary. Rather than describing the FCC process as nascent, management began characterizing it as progressing, with industry engagement and comment activity building. The opposition — Apple, NTIA, the Security Industry Association, WISPA, and the GPS Innovation Alliance, all filing comments citing 900 MHz interference concerns — was acknowledged but consistently framed as manageable friction rather than a structural barrier. Operationally, management noted that AT&T's continued deployment of Pinnacle under the existing operations agreement validated the commercial relevance of floor-level altitude positioning for the FirstNet public-safety network, even as it underscored the single-customer dependency that would become more acute in 2025.

## The Convertible Pivot: March 2025

The March 2025 earnings period brought a material narrative reset. The $190 million senior secured convertible note financing, which closed on March 27, 2025, was the largest capital event in NextNav's post-SPAC history. Led by M-Cor Capital — the Milken Family Office — and Fortress Investment Group affiliates, the transaction replaced the prior $70 million of 10% Senior Secured Notes due 2026 with $190 million of 5% notes due June 2028. The mechanics were straightforward: net proceeds of approximately $188.6 million redeemed the prior notes at 101 percent of par, reducing the annual cash interest burden and extending maturity by more than two years.

The strategic framing of the financing was, however, carefully constructed. Management positioned the transaction not as a dilutive capital raise but as a runway extension that funded the company through the anticipated FCC rulemaking timeline. With approximately $152 million in cash and short-term investments as of year-end 2025, NextNav had an estimated 18 to 24 months of operating runway beyond the close — a window that management argued aligned with the regulatory progression from Notice of Inquiry to Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to Final Rule. The participation of the Milken Family Office was cited as validation from sophisticated long-duration capital of the spectrum thesis's probability-weighted value.

The stock's reaction around the financing announcement and close was volatile. The convertible's $12.56 conversion price set a technical reference level, and the combination of refinancing relief and marquee investor participation provided a near-term catalyst. But the financing simultaneously confirmed what the market had suspected: at current revenue levels and burn rates, NextNav could not fund itself organically and required access to capital markets at significant dilution optionality for noteholders. The net loss for FY 2025 reached $189.3 million — approximately 2.7 times the operating loss of $70.2 million — driven largely by non-cash charges from derivative liability recognition and the accounting treatment of the note extinguishment.

## The Concentration Reckoning: Q3 2025

No single quarterly result in NextNav's post-IPO history concentrated the structural risk of the business model more starkly than Q3 2025. Total quarterly revenue fell to $887,000, with a single customer — AT&T — representing 89 percent of that figure. The disclosed concentration had always been a feature of the Pinnacle business model, but at this scale it crossed from notable into arresting. Management's language on the Q3 call navigated the tension between transparency and confidence: the revenue step-down was attributed to the phasing and milestone structure of the AT&T operations agreement rather than demand deterioration, and the October 2025 extension of the agreement through October 2028 was positioned as the definitive counterpoint to any concern about customer continuity.

The Q3 2025 period nevertheless represents the moment when the AT&T concentration transformed, in the earnings disclosure record, from a feature of a focused early-stage company into a formally disclosed and prominently foregrounded risk factor. The transition mattered not just for the income statement but for the credibility of the NextGen commercial thesis: if the entire existing revenue base rested on a single carrier agreement for a single E911 service, the argument that domestic mobile network operators would broadly license the NextGen platform required a more developed pipeline than management had yet been able to disclose.

## FCC Language Shifts: From Inquiry to NPRM

Tracking the regulatory language across quarters reveals a measurable tightening. Through 2023, the FCC process was described in terms of advocacy and petition-building. In the 2024 calls following the April petition filing, language shifted to "the process is progressing" and references to substantive comment activity. The March 2025 Notice of Inquiry — WT Docket No. 25-110 — gave management a concrete milestone to cite, and the tone shifted again: "formal FCC proceeding" replaced "petition" as the operative descriptor. By the time of the OMB notification of a pending NPRM in early 2026, management's language had moved to "regulatory catalyst" and "rulemaking timeline," signaling that the company believed it was past the initiating phase and into the substantive evaluation phase of the process.

The October 2025 simultaneous-transmission demonstration — proving that 5G PNT and standard carrier data traffic could coexist on NextNav's licensed spectrum using commercial 5G network equipment — was the technical proof point management had needed to support the interference-compatibility argument. The December 2025 MetCom licensing agreement in Japan provided international market validation. Both events were cited in subsequent calls as evidence that the NextGen platform had progressed from concept to demonstrated commercial-grade technology.

## Credibility Assessment: Consistency Against the Record

Against the documented regulatory milestones, NextNav's management narrative has been broadly consistent, if deliberately optimistic in tone. The regulatory progression — petition to NOI to NPRM notification — has tracked broadly within the windows management implied, though the company has been careful to avoid committing to specific NPRM or Final Rule dates. The technology demonstrations of late 2025 delivered on the proof-of-concept milestones management had telegraphed.

The area of greatest tension between narrative and reality is domestic commercial traction. The NextGen commercial thesis requires U.S. mobile network operators to license PNT technology into their 5G infrastructure — a step that remains undemonstrated in the earnings record as of the frozen snapshot date.

| Period | Revenue | Operating Loss | Key Narrative Theme |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | $3.9M | $63.5M | TerraPoiNT validation; federal contract |
| FY 2024 | $5.7M | $60.1M | FCC petition filed; Brattle $14.6B study |
| Q3 2025 | $0.9M | — | AT&T concentration disclosed at 89% |
| FY 2025 | $4.6M | $70.2M | $190M convertible; NOI issued; NextGen demo |
| ==Q1 2026== | ==$1.0M== | ==—== | ==OMB notification of pending NPRM; net loss $10.6M== |

Four forward markers will define whether the earnings narrative converts into commercial reality across the next four quarters: a domestic carrier licensing agreement for NextGen; a disclosed FCC NPRM issuance date; any second revenue-generating customer beyond AT&T; and management guidance on cash runway extension options if the June 2028 debt maturity approaches without a spectrum reconfiguration decision. The credibility accumulated across twelve quarters of consistent regulatory narrative is substantial — but the next four will test whether conviction and outcome remain aligned.

chapters.title: Sorond, Gray, and the Spectrum Lobby: How NextNav's Leadership Team Was Built for a Washington Outcome
chapters.body:
## A Management Team Built for Washington

Pick up NextNav's proxy statement and read the executive biographies in sequence. A CEO who advised the FCC and sits on the CTIA Board of Directors. A VP Regulatory Affairs who worked at the Office of Science and Technology Policy and the FCC before a stint at Google. A VP Government Affairs rated a "Top Lobbyist" by The Hill for three consecutive years. A CFO recruited directly from the single most structurally analogous 900 MHz spectrum company in the United States. The cumulative effect is striking: NextNav's leadership team reads less like the management of a technology company and more like the staff list of a well-funded spectrum policy advocacy organization that happens to have an engineering department attached.

That observation is not a criticism. It is a description of the company's theory of value creation. NextNav's commercial fate is determined by an FCC rulemaking, and the company assembled its executive bench accordingly. The technical platform — TerraPoiNT, NextGen, the 5G NR integration — is the product. But the product has no market until Washington says it does. Understanding who NextNav hired, and why, is inseparable from understanding what the company actually is.

## Mariam Sorond: Chairwoman, CEO, and Spectrum Policy Advocate in Chief

Mariam Sorond arrived at NextNav carrying nearly three decades of senior wireless industry experience across a career that moved through every layer of the mobile ecosystem. She served as VP Technology at DISH Network, an operator whose chronic ambitions in 5G spectrum deployment gave her a front-row view of how spectrum policy decisions translate — or fail to translate — into commercial outcomes. She moved to CableLabs as Chief Wireless Officer, working at the intersection of cable operators and wireless standards at a moment when the industry was negotiating 5G integration. At VMware, she held the title of Chief Research and Technology Officer for the telco and cloud service provider division, watching the virtualization of network functions accelerate toward the 5G NR core.

The through-line across all three employers is regulatory fluency. Spectrum is not an engineering problem in isolation; it is an engineering problem embedded inside a policy process governed by the FCC, the NTIA, and the White House — and Sorond accumulated advisory relationships with all three. Her position on the CTIA Board of Directors placed her in the room where the wireless industry's collective lobbying priorities were set. When NextNav needed a leader who could walk into the FCC and be taken seriously as a peer, Sorond's résumé was nearly purpose-built for the role.

Her appointment as both CEO and Board Chair raised governance questions that the proxy statement did not fully resolve. Concentrating executive authority and governance oversight in a single individual is unusual for a public company at any stage; for a pre-commercial company burning through cash at accelerating rates — net losses of $71.7 million in 2023, $101.9 million in 2024, and $189.3 million in 2025 — it is a structural choice that investors accepted without the counterweight of a strong independent board majority. The appointment of Lisa Hook as Lead Independent Director in February 2026 partially addressed that gap, but the dual role remained intact.

Sorond's public communications framed NextNav's mission in national-security terms that transcended the commercial context. GPS vulnerability — jamming, spoofing, the fragility of satellite signals in dense urban environments and contested battlespaces — was the existential threat her technology existed to solve. The framing was not merely marketing; it aligned NextNav's commercial interests with the explicit policy directives of the federal government, including White House Space Policy Directive 7 (2021), which mandated federal agencies to develop and deploy GPS alternatives. When Sorond spoke about spectrum reconfiguration before the FCC or in congressional briefings, she was speaking the language of national resilience, not quarterly revenue. Whether that framing was strategically effective would depend on whether the FCC agreed that NextNav's particular solution — a single company's licensed spectrum holdings — was the appropriate vessel for a national public good.

## Tim Gray and the Anterix Precedent

The September 2025 appointment of Tim Gray as Chief Financial Officer was the most strategically legible personnel move in NextNav's recent history. Gray spent more than a decade as CFO at Anterix, a company so structurally similar to NextNav that the comparison almost constitutes a controlled experiment.

Anterix held licensed 900 MHz spectrum — specifically in the 900 MHz band — and pursued a regulatory strategy to reposition that spectrum for private broadband networks serving utilities and critical infrastructure operators. Its commercial model was licensing-based: sell or lease spectrum usage rights to enterprise customers rather than build and operate networks directly. Its value was almost entirely a function of FCC proceedings that would allow it to reconfigure its spectrum holdings for modern broadband use. It was a small-cap company with a large regulatory bet and a balance sheet defined by the gap between its modest operating revenues and the optionality value embedded in its licensed spectrum.

Gray managed Anterix's finances through the years when that regulatory optionality was its primary asset and its liquidity runway was the critical variable. He understood how to manage a convertible note structure, how to communicate with institutional investors holding both debt and equity positions, and how to present a balance sheet in which the income statement was largely irrelevant to the investment thesis. He brought those skills directly to a company carrying $190 million in convertible notes due June 2028 — notes issued at a 5% coupon and a conversion price of $12.56 per share — at a moment when the distance between current operations and commercial viability remained measured in regulatory milestones rather than product shipments. Gray's predecessor Chris Gates did not exit the company; he moved to EVP Corporate Development, a title that typically signals active pursuit of M&A, licensing transactions, or spectrum portfolio deals. The reorganization suggested NextNav was simultaneously managing its existing capital structure and preparing for the business development work a favorable FCC ruling might require.

Gray's prior career included stints at MedImmune (later AstraZeneca), AOL, and Nextel — a roster that spans pharmaceutical royalty management, digital media, and mobile spectrum. But the Anterix decade was the credential that mattered. NextNav did not hire a CFO to run a conventional technology finance function. It hired someone who had already lived inside the specific financial architecture it was now navigating.

## Arun Raghupathy and the Technical Foundation

Against the backdrop of a leadership team oriented toward Washington, co-founder and SVP Technology Development Dr. Arun Raghupathy represented the engineering substance behind the regulatory argument. With backgrounds at Qualcomm and Texas Instruments in GNSS chipsets and wireless systems, Raghupathy was part of the original founding group that established the technical thesis: GPS fails indoors, in urban canyons, and in contested environments; a terrestrial broadcast network on licensed spectrum can fill the gap. He held more than fifty patents and served as the technical architect of both TerraPoiNT and the NextGen 5G PNT architecture.

The external validation benchmark for Raghupathy's work arrived in 2021, when the U.S. Department of Transportation evaluated multiple alternative PNT technologies in a formal testing program. TerraPoiNT ranked as the top-performing system across all evaluation metrics — accuracy, resilience, coverage, and timing synchronization. That result was the credential NextNav cited in virtually every regulatory filing and investor presentation thereafter. Raghupathy's team also achieved better than 50 nanoseconds timing synchronization accuracy in demonstrations, performance relevant to 5G network synchronization requirements and to financial trading infrastructure, where GPS timing underpins exchange operations. The October 2025 simultaneous-transmission demonstration — 5G positioning and standard uplink/downlink data on the same commercial base station equipment — was the most recent milestone his team delivered.

## Board Architecture: Fortress, Milken, and the Question of Independence

The board reflected the capital structure more than it concealed it. Fortress Investment Group had been a NextNav investor since the pre-IPO venture rounds, participated in the $190 million March 2025 convertible financing alongside M-Cor Capital (the Milken Family Office), and held board-influencing positions. The overlap between debt holder, equity holder, and board-influencer is common in pre-commercial companies dependent on institutional capital for survival, but it creates an alignment question: Fortress and M-Cor held convertible notes with a June 2028 maturity and a $12.56 conversion price. Their incentives around the timing and terms of any FCC regulatory outcome, any capital raise, or any strategic transaction were not necessarily identical to those of common shareholders holding equity at a market capitalization that exceeded $2 billion against $4.6 million in annual revenue.

The February 2026 appointment of Lisa Hook as Lead Independent Director addressed the most visible governance gap. Hook had served as CEO of Neustar, a company that made its business operating critical national telecommunications infrastructure — specifically the Number Portability Administration Center (NPAC), the system that routes phone calls when customers switch carriers — under government mandate. The Neustar analogy was more than résumé decoration. Neustar demonstrated that a private company could hold and operate a piece of national communications infrastructure under a government-mandated framework, generating durable revenue from the structural necessity of the service.
