NextNav's aspiration to become national PNT infrastructure — the terrestrial GPS backup that carriers, emergency services, and federal agencies would rely on — was exactly the model Neustar had executed in a different domain. Hook's committee assignments (Technology and National Defense; Compensation and Human Capital) placed her expertise where it was most operationally relevant.

## Renee Gregory, Ed Mortimer, and the Regulatory Apparatus

The regulatory affairs team's seniority relative to NextNav's revenue scale would be remarkable at any company. Renee Gregory, VP Regulatory Affairs, brought experience from the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the FCC, and Google — a career arc through the institutions that set federal technology and spectrum policy, followed by time at the private-sector actor most affected by FCC decisions on the mobile internet. Ed Mortimer, VP Government Affairs, had spent more than thirty years in government affairs, including tenure at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, and earned recognition as a Top Lobbyist by The Hill for three consecutive years.

At a company generating $4.6 million in annual revenue, the compensation cost of retaining two executives of that seniority in Washington-facing roles was significant in proportion to total operating scale. That allocation decision revealed something important about the company's self-understanding. NextNav did not budget like a technology company waiting for its regulatory approval to arrive. It budgeted like an organization that believed its primary work product was influence — regulatory credibility, stakeholder relationships, and the conversion of a technical capability into a policy outcome. Whether that was a strength — deep Washington access at the moment the FCC was conducting its most consequential spectrum inquiry in a decade — or a signal of the company's frank acknowledgment that it had no path to value without a favorable ruling, was a question the FCC's eventual decision on WT Docket No. 25-110 would answer.

chapters.title: AT&T, The Pentagon, and the 911 Mandate: NextNav's Customer Base Across Public Safety, Federal, and Prospective Carrier Markets
chapters.body:
## The 89 Percent Problem

Few technology companies with market capitalizations above $2 billion face a customer concentration as acute as NextNav's. In the third quarter of 2025, a single customer — AT&T — accounted for approximately 89 percent of the company's quarterly revenue. Total revenue in that quarter was $887,000. The arithmetic is unforgiving: AT&T's Pinnacle operations agreement was not merely NextNav's largest contract. It was effectively the entire business.

The agreement, formally structured as a network operations arrangement covering AT&T's FirstNet public-safety broadband network, carries an October 2028 termination date following a two-year extension executed in October 2025. That term provides a contractual runway. It does not eliminate the fundamental counterparty risk. Were AT&T to elect termination, invoke any material breach provision, or simply allow the agreement to lapse without renewal, NextNav's revenue base — already generating just $4.6 million in full-year 2025 — would collapse to amounts that could not sustain even a skeleton operating structure. The company's [2025 10-K filed with the SEC](https://ir.nextnav.com/financial-information/sec-filings) lists the concentration explicitly as a material risk factor, with the acknowledgment that the loss of AT&T would have a "material adverse effect" on the business. Given the revenue figures involved, that disclosure understates the operational reality.

## AT&T, FirstNet, and the Mandate That Created Pinnacle

The AT&T relationship did not arise from commercial competition. It arose from regulation.

Beginning in 2015, the FCC began imposing increasingly stringent location accuracy requirements on wireless carriers for Enhanced 911 services. The initial mandates addressed horizontal accuracy — latitude and longitude positioning for emergency calls — but a growing body of evidence, including research commissioned by the National Emergency Number Association, demonstrated that in multi-story urban buildings, horizontal coordinates alone were functionally useless for first responders. A 911 call from a building at a known street address could originate from the ground floor or the thirty-second floor; without z-axis data, paramedics and police searched floor by floor.

The FCC's z-axis accuracy mandates, phased in from 2021, required carriers to demonstrate floor-level accuracy for indoor wireless 911 calls in the largest U.S. markets. NextNav's Pinnacle system was designed from the outset to solve precisely this problem. The platform aggregates barometric pressure readings from smartphone sensors and cross-references them against a nationwide network of calibrated reference pressure sensors installed in commercial buildings across more than 4,400 U.S. cities, covering more than 90 percent of commercial structures taller than three stories. The output is a floor-level altitude fix appended to the 911 location data transmitted to Public Safety Answering Points.

AT&T, as the operator of FirstNet — the congressionally mandated, FCC-licensed dedicated broadband network for first responders — became the natural anchor customer. FirstNet's mission alignment with E911 accuracy made the Pinnacle integration both commercially rational and publicly defensible. The Pinnacle service is delivered through the FirstNet infrastructure, and the agreement's milestone-based payment structure explains the volatility in NextNav's reported quarterly revenue. The 46 percent year-over-year revenue growth in fiscal 2024, followed by a 19 percent decline in fiscal 2025 to $4.6 million, reflects not underlying demand fluctuation but the recognition cadence of milestone payments under the contract's architecture — a dynamic that makes trailing revenue figures unreliable as indicators of the relationship's durability.

The October 2025 extension through October 2028 was the clearest available signal that AT&T views Pinnacle as a continuing compliance necessity rather than a transitional workaround. FCC z-axis mandates remain in force. The regulatory driver that created the contract has not diminished.

## Washington as Customer and Validator

NextNav's second customer category carries smaller current revenue but considerably larger strategic significance. In November 2023, the company signed a contract with an unnamed federal agency for GPS and PNT characterization services — work that drew on TerraPoiNT's capability to operate as a functional GPS analog using terrestrially broadcast signals on licensed 920–928 MHz spectrum at power levels approximately 10,000 times greater than GPS satellite signals received at ground level.

The national security context that animates federal interest in TerraPoiNT is not hypothetical. GPS jamming and spoofing incidents documented in Eastern Europe — including interference affecting commercial aviation operating near the Baltic states and Finland — and in the Middle East have demonstrated that satellite-only PNT infrastructure represents a systemic vulnerability. The incidents accelerated Congressional and executive branch attention to alternative PNT architectures that could not be neutralized by adversary electronic warfare at GPS frequencies.

The policy response crystallized in the White House Space Policy Directive 7, signed in 2021, which directed federal agencies to assess GPS dependencies and develop backup PNT capabilities. In the same year, the U.S. Department of Transportation conducted a formal comparative evaluation of alternative PNT technologies to identify GPS complements suitable for national infrastructure applications. TerraPoiNT ranked first among all evaluated solutions across the DoT's assessment criteria. Timing synchronization demonstrations subsequently achieved accuracy better than 50 nanoseconds — performance relevant not only to positioning but to the precise timing requirements of financial settlement systems, power grid management, and 5G network synchronization that are currently satellite-dependent.

The November 2023 federal contract did not translate into material disclosed revenue. But the DoT ranking and the federal characterization agreement collectively established NextNav as a credible vendor in the government PNT procurement pipeline — a validation that the company's regulatory filings cite as evidence of institutional demand independent of the commercial carrier market.

## MetCom and the International Template

The December 2025 agreement with MetCom International of Tokyo provided the clearest preview yet of how NextNav intends to monetize the NextGen 5G platform internationally. MetCom licensed NextNav's 5G-based 3D PNT waveform and receiver technologies — the core intellectual property underpinning the NextGen platform — for deployment across Japan's largest metropolitan areas, subject to Japanese regulatory approval.

The structure is instructive. NextNav is not building or operating a network in Japan. MetCom, a Japanese company with existing relationships in that market's regulatory and telecommunications environment, assumes the network deployment and operational burden. NextNav's contribution is the technology license: the 5G Positioning Reference Signal waveform design, the receiver algorithms developed through the Nestwave SAS acquisition in November 2022, and the standards work that embeds PNT capability into 5G NR infrastructure. The arrangement converts NextNav from a capital-intensive network operator into a technology licensor — a model that, if replicated across multiple international markets, generates royalty-type revenue without the balance sheet burden of building TerraPoiNT-equivalent transmitter networks from scratch.

Japan's urban density makes the market a logical first international deployment. Tokyo, Osaka, and Nagoya are among the densest environments in the world for GPS signal attenuation, and Japan has a documented national interest in GPS resilience following the March 2011 earthquake, which highlighted emergency communications vulnerabilities. MetCom's willingness to license and deploy the technology before FCC spectrum reconfiguration is resolved in the United States provides partial validation that NextNav's technology has standalone commercial value beyond its domestic spectrum position.

## The MNO Gap: What FCC Approval Would Unlock

The prospective domestic mobile network operator market is, by NextNav's own framing, the central commercial opportunity created by the NextGen platform. The thesis is straightforward: major U.S. carriers already operate dense 5G NR infrastructure. ~~NextNav holds licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population.~~ ==NextNav holds 8 MHz of contiguous licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population, plus 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the population.== If the FCC's spectrum reconfiguration proceeding (WT Docket No. 25-110) proceeds to a Final Rule creating a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use license for 5G NR operations, carriers could integrate NextNav's PNT technology into their existing base stations using NextNav's spectrum, delivering positioning and timing services via 5G Positioning Reference Signals without building new network infrastructure.

As of the May 2026 frozen snapshot date, no domestic MNO licensing agreement beyond the AT&T Pinnacle contract had been announced. The barriers are multiple and reinforcing. Absent FCC approval of the spectrum reconfiguration, carriers cannot legally operate 5G NR services on NextNav's current M-LMS licensed frequencies — the existing license class does not permit it. The regulatory condition precedent is absolute. Beyond spectrum authorization, carriers face integration complexity: embedding a third-party PNT layer into 5G NR standards-compliant equipment requires chipset support, software stack modifications, and inter-vendor coordination that represents non-trivial engineering and commercial negotiation. The October 2025 demonstration of simultaneous 5G data and PNT signal transmission on commercial equipment was the technical proof-of-concept; it was not a commercial deployment.

The FCC opposition mounted by Apple, NTIA, the Security Industry Association, WISPA, and the GPS Innovation Alliance — primarily centered on interference concerns for the hundreds of millions of consumer and industrial devices operating in the 900 MHz band — adds regulatory risk that rational carrier procurement decisions appropriately discount until the rulemaking outcome is known. Signing a licensing agreement with NextNav before spectrum reconfiguration is approved would expose a carrier to regulatory and capital risk with no certain deployment path.

## From ~~$887,000~~ ==$995,000== to $14.6 Billion: The Market Sizing Gap

The contrast between NextNav's current revenue and its claimed total addressable market requires no literary embellishment.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| ~~Q3 2025 quarterly revenue~~ ==Q1 2026 quarterly revenue== | ~~$887,000~~ ==$995,000== |
| FY 2025 annual revenue | $4.6 million |
| AT&T revenue concentration (Q3 2025) | ~89% |
| Brattle Group economic value estimate (spectrum reconfiguration) | $14.6 billion total; $10.8 billion GPS outage insurance value |
| Market capitalization (approximately, May 2026) | ~$2.2–$2.5 billion |

The Brattle Group analysis, commissioned in connection with NextNav's April 2024 FCC Petition for Rulemaking, estimated $14.6 billion in total economic value from spectrum reconfiguration — comprising direct network value, GPS outage insurance against infrastructure disruption, and the operational savings to federal, commercial, and public-safety users from having a robust domestic GPS complement. White House Space Policy Directive 7 and the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act's provisions on GPS resilience provide the federal demand signal. The MetCom agreement establishes the international licensing model. And the AT&T Pinnacle extension through 2028 provides a minimum revenue floor that keeps the lights on while the FCC rulemaking proceeds.

The gap between those data points — ~~$887,000~~ ==$995,000== in quarterly revenue and a multi-billion-dollar market potential — is the entirety of NextNav's investment proposition. The company's customer base today is, in functional terms, one carrier, one regulatory mandate, and an emerging federal relationship. Whether that base expands to encompass domestic MNOs, additional federal contracts, and international licensees beyond MetCom depends almost entirely on a regulatory proceeding that NextNav cannot control, against opposition it cannot fully neutralize, on a timeline measured not in quarters but in years.

chapters.title: The GPS Alternatives Landscape: NextNav's Spectrum Moat Against Iridium STL, eLoran, and the 5G Positioning Ecosystem
chapters.body:
## Two Rings of Competition

NextNav operates in two distinct competitive arenas that are related but not identical. The first is the contest among alternative Positioning, Navigation, and Timing technologies to serve as the designated complement or backup to GPS for U.S. national infrastructure — a market shaped almost entirely by federal policy, defense procurement, and the White House's Space Policy Directive 7 mandate. The second is the commercial market for indoor and urban location services: the E911 altitude accuracy business that Pinnacle currently monetises through AT&T, and the broader enterprise and carrier positioning market that the NextGen platform targets. Each arena has its own cast of competitors, and the dynamics in one heavily influence the other.

## Satelles: Rival or Partner?

The most technically credible alternative PNT system operating at national scale is Satelles and its Satellite Time and Location service, which broadcast timing and positioning signals through the Iridium low-Earth orbit constellation. STL's central advantage is geographic ubiquity: the Iridium constellation provides polar and equatorial coverage without the terrestrial infrastructure investment that TerraPoiNT requires. For outdoor timing applications — synchronising telecommunications networks, financial exchanges, or energy grid nodes — STL delivers sub-microsecond accuracy from a hardened, space-based asset.

The comparison with NextNav, however, reveals a fundamental physical asymmetry. Iridium satellites orbit at roughly 780 kilometres, and their signals arrive at ground level at power levels only modestly better than GPS — and still many orders of magnitude weaker than a terrestrial 900 MHz transmitter operating at close range. NextNav's TerraPoiNT, by contrast, broadcasts at approximately 10,000 times the effective received power of GPS. That power differential is decisive for indoor and urban-canyon penetration, where signal attenuation through steel-frame buildings, reinforced concrete, and dense urban geometry renders LEO-based signals unreliable or unavailable. Satelles openly acknowledges this limitation: STL is positioned as a timing and coarse-positioning service for outdoor and lightly-shielded environments, not a floor-level altitude solution for 911 callers inside high-rise buildings.

The competitive overlap is therefore narrower than it first appears, and both companies recognised this. NextNav and Satelles collaborated on a joint alternative PNT testbed in the San Francisco Bay Area — a demonstration of complementarity rather than zero-sum rivalry. In the federal PNT resilience framework, the dominant architecture envisioned by most technical stakeholders involves layered diversity: no single alternative replaces GPS, but a combination of terrestrial and satellite-based backups produces a system more robust than any single technology. In that framing, Satelles is less a competitor than a co-occupant of the alternative PNT ecosystem, serving different environmental niches and, potentially, different federal procurement programmes.

## eLoran: The Legacy Contender

Enhanced long-range navigation — eLoran — represents the only alternative PNT technology with a longer U.S. policy history than NextNav. Operating at 100 kHz, eLoran transmitters broadcast at extremely high power across intercontinental distances, providing timing accuracy on the order of 50–100 nanoseconds and coarse positioning accuracy measured in tens of metres. The United States operated a Loran-C network until its decommissioning in 2010; a small but persistent coalition of advocates, led by UrsaNav and supported periodically by the Coast Guard and some elements of the Department of Homeland Security, has pressed for an eLoran network to be rebuilt as a national GPS backup.

Against NextNav, eLoran's limitations are structural. At 100 kHz, the signal bandwidth is narrow, constraining positioning precision in urban environments. More critically, at very low frequency the signal propagates primarily along the ground wave and surface, making it poorly suited to the vertical (z-axis) positioning that is the core of Pinnacle's E911 value proposition. Indoor penetration at 100 kHz is theoretically good for shielded environments, but the technology lacks the signal geometry — from a small number of widely-spaced transmitters — to resolve fine-grained 3D coordinates in dense urban settings. eLoran's political durability rests on its low infrastructure cost relative to national coverage and its interoperability with maritime navigation, not on any performance advantage over terrestrial 900 MHz broadcasts.

The more relevant competitive dynamic between eLoran and NextNav is at the level of Washington politics. eLoran proponents and NextNav's FCC rulemaking strategy effectively compete for the same finite legislative and regulatory bandwidth — the attention of Congressional staffers, NTIA officials, and FCC commissioners concerned about GPS resilience. To the extent that eLoran advocacy positions itself as the cheaper, proven, build-it-now solution, it absorbs political energy that might otherwise accelerate the FCC's WT Docket No. 25-110 rulemaking. NextNav's rebuttal has been consistent: eLoran is a legacy maritime technology without the 3D accuracy, spectrum integration, or 5G scalability that a modern national PNT backbone demands.

## Orolia/Safran: The Defense Niche

Orolia, acquired by Safran in 2022 and now marketed under the Safran Trusted 4D brand, operates in the resilient PNT space primarily as a defence and critical-infrastructure supplier. Its VersaPNT platform integrates GPS, inertial navigation, and alternative signal sources into hardened receivers designed for military vehicles, shipboard systems, and secure ground installations. Safran also manufactures GNSS signal simulators and jamming-detection systems used by defence agencies for testing and vulnerability assessment.

The competitive overlap with NextNav is real but bounded. In federal defence procurement — where programme offices are evaluating GPS-alternative receivers for tactical platforms — both companies compete for specification inclusion and system integration contracts. But Safran's go-to-market model is hardware-centric and defence-focused, while NextNav's NextGen strategy is predicated on software integration into commercial 5G carrier infrastructure and licensing revenue. They occupy different positions in the procurement supply chain: Safran sells receivers; NextNav aspires to sell spectrum-and-platform access. This distinction makes direct competition less acute than the shared policy arena might suggest.

## The 5G Positioning Challenge

The most structurally significant competitive threat to NextNav's long-term differentiation did not arrive from legacy navigation companies. It arrived from the 3GPP standards body. Starting with Release 16 (2020) and extended through Release 17 and beyond, 5G New Radio specifications introduced a suite of native positioning methods: Observed Time Difference of Arrival (OTDOA), Uplink Time Difference of Arrival (UTDOA), Angle of Arrival (AoA), and Round-Trip Time (RTT) measurements. Qualcomm and other chipmakers moved quickly to embed these methods in commercial modems. As 5G NR infrastructure density grows — particularly in urban environments where small cells are deployed at close spacing — the geometric precision available from 5G NR positioning without any dedicated spectrum improves materially.

The critical question is whether 5G NR positioning, built on licensed carrier spectrum already deployed, can eventually deliver indoor accuracy comparable to what NextNav promises on its dedicated 900 MHz holdings. The honest answer, as of the frozen snapshot, is: not yet, but the trajectory matters. 3GPP Release 17 targets sub-metre horizontal accuracy under idealised conditions; real-world indoor performance depends heavily on cell density, multipath conditions, and device-side calibration. NextNav's 920–928 MHz propagation has meaningful physical advantages in building penetration and signal strength uniformity relative to mid-band 5G frequencies. But as carrier infrastructure densifies and 5G positioning algorithms mature, the performance gap that justifies a separate licensed overlay network may narrow over time.

This is the competitive scenario NextNav's NextGen platform is explicitly designed to pre-empt — not by resisting 5G NR positioning, but by becoming part of it. By embedding PNT broadcasts as Positioning Reference Signals on licensed 900 MHz spectrum into standard 5G base stations, NextGen attempts to make NextNav's spectrum a native component of the carrier network rather than a competing overlay.

## The FCC Opposition: Competitive Camouflage?

The alignment of opponents in NextNav's FCC proceeding merits scrutiny. Apple, the GPS Innovation Alliance, WISPA, and the Security Industry Association each filed opposition citing interference concerns — specifically, potential degradation to 900 MHz consumer devices including agricultural sensors, industrial telemetry, and unlicensed low-power devices that share the band. The interference argument is technically substantive and not merely pretextual: the 902–928 MHz band is populated with heterogeneous incumbents, and any reconfiguration creates genuine coordination complexity.

But the opposition coalition also has strategic texture. Apple has invested substantially in its own indoor positioning infrastructure through the Find My network — a dense mesh of Bluetooth-enabled devices that provides crowdsourced indoor location at no incremental spectrum cost. A federally-mandated GPS backup standard built on NextNav's licensed spectrum would be, at minimum, a competing reference infrastructure for indoor location. Whether Apple's opposition reflects interference engineering concern, competitive self-interest, or both, the effect is the same: it adds procedural mass to the FCC rulemaking and extends the timeline.

## The Spectrum Moat

Across all competitive dimensions, NextNav's most durable advantage returns to a single asset: ~~12 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population, supplemented by an additional 4 MHz of complementary lower 900 MHz spectrum covering part of the U.S. population==, held under Mobile Location and Monitoring Service licences that no competitor can replicate without independent regulatory action. Satelles cannot relocate LEO satellites; eLoran proponents cannot requisition 900 MHz spectrum; 5G carrier positioning operates on spectrum the carriers already own, which is neither in the 900 MHz band nor licensed for the specific PNT use case NextNav is pursuing.

The spectrum moat is real. Its sufficiency as a long-term competitive differentiator depends on one condition: whether the FCC reconfiguration that transforms M-LMS licences into flexible-use 5G NR-capable spectrum is actually granted. Without that rulemaking outcome, the moat surrounds territory whose commercial value remains largely theoretical. With it, NextNav holds a nationwide licensed PNT infrastructure position that, as CEO Mariam Sorond has argued repeatedly, simply cannot be replicated by any private entity starting from scratch — regardless of capital or technology. The spectrum moat is the argument. The FCC proceeding is the verdict.

chapters.title: From FCC Petition to OMB NPRM Notice: The 2024–2026 Regulatory and Commercial Catalyst Timeline
chapters.body:
## The Petition That Started the Clock

On April 2024, NextNav filed a Petition for Rulemaking with the Federal Communications Commission that transformed the company's regulatory posture from passive spectrum holder to active architect of national policy. The petition requested a fundamental reconfiguration of the lower 900 MHz band — the 902–928 MHz block where NextNav holds its Mobile Location and Monitoring Service licences — ~~creating a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use allocation structured as paired 5 MHz uplink and 10 MHz downlink channels plus an additional 5 MHz, all suitable for 5G New Radio operations~~ ==creating a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use allocation structured as a 5 MHz uplink at 902–907 MHz paired with a 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz, suitable for 5G New Radio operations==. The framing was deliberate and politically loaded: NextNav positioned the proposal not as a spectrum grab but as a national security imperative.

Accompanying the petition was an independent economic analysis by [The Brattle Group](https://www.brattle.com/) estimating the reconfiguration would generate $14.6 billion in total economic value to the United States, of which $10.8 billion represented what the consultancy characterised as GPS outage insurance value — the avoided cost of disruptions to logistics, financial systems, and critical infrastructure in scenarios of sustained GPS jamming or spoofing. The remaining $3.8 billion reflected commercial PNT service revenues and productivity gains. The political backdrop could not have been more favourable: GPS jamming incidents in Eastern Europe and the Middle East had proliferated, aviation authorities were documenting spoofing events near conflict zones with increasing frequency, and the White House Space Policy Directive 7 of 2021 had already mandated federal agencies to develop and implement GPS alternatives. NextNav was presenting itself as the answer Congress and the executive branch were implicitly demanding.

## The Comment Period: Organised Opposition, Expected Friction

The FCC's decision to seek public comment opened a formal window that ran through late August and September 2024, drawing hundreds of filers — a volume that itself signalled how consequential the spectrum community regarded the proceeding. The opposition coalesced around a coalition whose names carried institutional weight: Apple, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, the Security Industry Association, the Wireless Internet Service Providers Association, and the GPS Innovation Alliance all filed comments raising interference concerns with the proposed reconfiguration. The core objection was technical: the 900 MHz band hosts an established ecosystem of low-power devices, short-range industrial sensors, and unlicensed equipment operating under part-15 rules, and opponents contended that broadcasting high-power 5G NR signals on adjacent or co-channel spectrum could degrade or destroy those incumbents.

The opposition was substantively predictable rather than damaging to NextNav's core regulatory argument. Any spectrum rulemaking of this scale attracts interference objections from incumbents who stand to lose operating margin in adjacent bands; the FCC's standard analytical framework addresses such claims through engineering studies and guard-band requirements rather than outright denial. More revealing was what the comments did not do: none of the major filers disputed the premise that GPS vulnerability constituted a genuine national security problem requiring a terrestrial solution. The debate was about mechanism and interference budget, not about whether the goal was legitimate. For NextNav, that was an acceptable place for the argument to stand.

## March 2025: The NOI Validates the Thesis

The Federal Communications Commission's issuance of a [Notice of Inquiry in WT Docket No. 25-110](https://www.fcc.gov/), titled *Promoting the Development of Positioning, Navigation, and Timing Technologies and Solutions*, in March 2025 represented the single most significant regulatory milestone in NextNav's history. The NOI was not an approval — it was a formal acknowledgment by the nation's primary spectrum regulator that GPS backup and complement infrastructure was a policy need requiring investigation. In spectrum rulemaking, an NOI is the opening of the funnel: it establishes the docket, invites further technical record-building, and positions the agency to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking once sufficient record exists to justify a proposed rule.

The market read the NOI as validation. NextNav's equity, which had already moved on the petition filing in 2024, reflected growing institutional conviction that the regulatory pathway was real rather than aspirational. The stock would trade between $10.84 and $24.19 over the twelve months following the NOI — a range that captured the binary character of the underlying bet, compressing toward the lower bound during periods of FCC silence and expanding when news flow was positive.

## The $190 Million Financing: Runway Meets Rulemaking

Eleven days before the close of March 2025, NextNav locked a $190 million senior secured convertible note financing that effectively synchronised the company's financial runway with the rulemaking timeline. The notes carried a 5% coupon, matured in June 2028, and converted at $12.56 per share — a meaningful premium to prevailing trading levels at issuance. The transaction was led by [M-Cor Capital](https://www.milken.com/), the Milken Family Office, alongside affiliates of [Fortress Investment Group](https://www.fortress.com/), which had been a NextNav investor since the pre-IPO period. Net proceeds of approximately $188.6 million were deployed in part to redeem the prior $70 million of 10% Senior Secured Notes due 2026 at 101% of par, cutting annual cash interest burden while extending debt maturity by over two years.

The financing carried a strategic signal beyond its financial mechanics. Fortress and Milken are not passive capital allocators; their willingness to roll prior debt into new convertible paper at lower yield — accepting equity upside rather than demanding higher coupons — reflected a judgment that the spectrum rulemaking had moved from speculative to probable. As of December 31, 2025, NextNav held approximately $152.2 million in cash and short-term investments, management guiding that the position funded operations beyond twelve months and creating an implied runway into mid-to-late 2027.

## Autumn 2025: Spectrum, Carrier, and Technology Proof Points

The autumn of 2025 delivered three catalysts in rapid sequence. In September, NextNav closed the acquisition of additional lower 900 MHz licences ~~that expanded its total contiguous holdings from 8 MHz to 12 MHz, covering more than 90% of the U.S. population,~~ ==that added roughly 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the U.S. population on top of the existing 8 MHz contiguous block reaching more than 90% of the population, lifting the total lower 900 MHz footprint to 12 MHz,== for consideration of up to $50 million. ~~Broader spectrum holdings directly strengthened the FCC reconfiguration case by demonstrating that NextNav could serve as a single nationwide licensee — the regulatory structure the petition had proposed — rather than a patchwork operator.~~ ==The expanded footprint strengthened the FCC reconfiguration case by deepening NextNav's position within the band the petition sought to restructure, even though the added 4 MHz was complementary rather than nationwide.== In October, AT&T extended its Pinnacle network operations agreement through October 2028, securing the revenue floor and signalling continued carrier confidence in NextNav's E911 infrastructure. That same month, NextNav demonstrated simultaneous delivery of accurate timing and positioning data alongside standard 5G uplink and downlink traffic on commercial 5G network equipment — the technical proof-of-concept that the NextGen platform could be embedded in existing carrier infrastructure without requiring a parallel standalone build.

December 2025 added the first international dimension when NextNav signed a strategic technology licensing agreement with MetCom International of Tokyo, granting rights to the NextGen 5G waveform and receiver technologies for deployment across Japan's largest metropolitan areas, subject to Japanese regulatory approval. The MetCom deal did not move near-term revenue — recognition would be deferred pending the regulatory process in Japan — but it demonstrated that a sophisticated foreign infrastructure operator had evaluated NextNav's technology and concluded it was commercially deployable.

February 2026 brought a governance signal: the appointment of Lisa Hook to the NextNav board of directors. Hook's prior leadership of Neustar — a company that managed critical communications infrastructure under federal mandate — and her familiarity with the intersection of telecommunications regulation and national security carried clear relevance for a company whose commercial fate rested on a Washington policy decision.

## The Forward Catalyst Stack as of May 2026

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the regulatory machinery remained in motion without resolution. The most significant forward binary was the FCC's issuance of a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in WT Docket No. 25-110 — the formal step that would publish a specific rule proposal for further comment and begin the clock on a potential Final Rule. The NPRM had been noticed to the Office of Management and Budget in early 2026, indicating that the commission had circulated draft language for inter-agency review, but publication in the Federal Register had not yet occurred within the frozen window.

Alongside the NPRM, Congressional attention to GPS resilience had produced active legislative proposals in both chambers — Senate and House bills directing federal agencies to accelerate procurement and deployment of GPS alternative infrastructure — that, if enacted, could mandate agency adoption of certified terrestrial PNT solutions and create a funded federal customer pipeline independent of the commercial carrier licensing thesis.

Domestically, the absence of a second U.S. mobile network operator licensing agreement remained the most conspicuous gap in NextNav's commercial narrative. The MetCom deal was international; the AT&T relationship covered only Pinnacle's E911 altitude service rather than the NextGen 5G PNT platform. A domestic MNO announcement — from any major carrier — would represent qualitative validation that the carrier integration pathway was commercially viable rather than theoretically plausible.

~~Finally, the filing of the FY 2025 Form 10-K and the Q1 2026 earnings report would provide the market with updated revenue, cash burn, and management commentary on the regulatory timeline — the routine financial disclosures that, for a company trading at more than 350 times trailing revenue, function as sentiment anchors around which the binary regulatory thesis resolves quarter by quarter.~~ ==Finally, with the FY 2025 Form 10-K and Q1 2026 earnings already on the tape — Q1 2026 revenue of $995 thousand against a $10.6 million net loss — subsequent quarterly disclosures would provide the market with updated revenue, cash burn, and management commentary on the regulatory timeline, the routine financial releases that, for a company trading at more than 350 times trailing revenue, function as sentiment anchors around which the binary regulatory thesis resolves quarter by quarter.==

chapters.title: Patents, Waveforms, and Trade Secrets: NextNav's Intellectual Property and R&D Architecture
chapters.body:
## Two Moats, One Company

NextNav's intellectual property position rests on a distinction most technology investors initially miss: the company's competitive advantage is constructed in two separate and independently valuable layers, neither of which automatically implies the other.

The first layer is regulatory rather than technical. NextNav's Mobile Location and Monitoring Service licenses covering ~~12 MHz of lower 900 MHz spectrum (902–928 MHz)~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum (920–928 MHz) reaching more than 90% of the U.S. population, plus an additional 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the U.S. population,== represent a scarce, governmentally-granted right to transmit across a licensed band at power levels capable of penetrating urban structures — an authorization that no amount of engineering ingenuity can replicate without a multi-year FCC proceeding. These licenses predated many of NextNav's foundational patents and would retain market value even if every NextNav patent were invalidated tomorrow.

The second layer is technical: more than 50 patents covering TerraPoiNT's signal architecture, Pinnacle's barometric reference network algorithms, and the NextGen 5G PNT waveform design — accumulated over nearly two decades under co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Dr. Arun Raghupathy. Those patents would carry meaningful licensing value independent of spectrum. A competitor holding a comparable spectrum position could not simply replicate NextNav's terrestrial positioning performance without navigating this estate.

The interaction between the two layers defines NextNav's structural position. A rival seeking to build a competing terrestrial GPS complement would need both a comparable spectrum license and the engineering depth to develop equivalent signal-processing and network-calibration capabilities without infringing existing NextNav IP. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, no announced competitor had assembled both.

## The Raghupathy Portfolio

Raghupathy's patent portfolio spans three distinct technical domains. The first covers TerraPoiNT's transmission and synchronization architecture: the methods by which ground-based transmitters achieve sub-50-nanosecond timing accuracy across a geographically distributed network, enabling the system to serve as a precision timing reference for telecommunications, financial, and national-security applications. The second covers Pinnacle's barometric pressure differential algorithms — the techniques for translating smartphone pressure sensor readings into floor-level altitude estimates calibrated against NextNav's fixed reference sensors across more than 4,400 U.S. cities. The third, and most commercially consequential, addresses receiver-side signal processing: the methods allowing a device to derive precise location data from terrestrial broadcasts in GPS-denied environments.

It was this third domain where the November 2022 acquisition of Nestwave SAS made its decisive contribution.

## The Nestwave Integration: Receiver Intelligence Meets Licensed Spectrum

Nestwave, headquartered in Neuilly-sur-Seine and staffed by engineers with deep roots in European 4G/5G receiver design, held a portfolio of patents covering signal-processing techniques that extract positioning data from existing LTE and 5G network transmissions — signals not originally designed for precision positioning. Nestwave's innovation was not a new over-the-air waveform but a receiver architecture for identifying and exploiting positioning-relevant characteristics in standardized cellular signals: multipath discrimination, timing reference extraction, and angle-of-arrival estimation from commercial base station emissions.

Integrated with NextNav's licensed 900 MHz spectrum holdings, this receiver intelligence achieved something neither asset could accomplish alone. TerraPoiNT's high-power terrestrial transmissions on dedicated licensed spectrum provided a robust, interference-resistant positioning signal. Nestwave's processing algorithms provided the efficiency to extract accurate position fixes without requiring specialized chipsets — enabling integration into standard commercial 5G baseband hardware. The combined capability formed the technical foundation for the NextGen platform's central commercial proposition: that mobile network operators could embed precision PNT into existing 5G infrastructure without commissioning a standalone network overlay.

NextNav characterized this integration as enabling an estimated 75% reduction in nationwide deployment costs — a figure that, applied against the capital expenditure baseline for a standalone TerraPoiNT buildout, implies savings exceeding $250 million. That estimate is company-attributed and not independently audited. The December 2025 MetCom International licensing agreement, covering deployment across Japan's major metropolitan areas, provided the first third-party commercial evidence that the combined IP package commanded market-rate licensing terms.

## R&D Expenditure: Burning Toward NextGen

NextNav's research and development spending reflected the company's transition from infrastructure operation to platform development across the 2023–2025 fiscal period. Net losses ran at $71.7 million in FY 2023, $101.9 million in FY 2024, and $189.3 million in FY 2025 — an acceleration driven materially by deepening NextGen platform investment. Against FY 2025 revenue of $4.6 million, the R&D burn rate placed NextNav structurally among pre-commercial semiconductor or wireless infrastructure companies, not mature software providers. The NextGen 5G platform consumed the dominant share of engineering resources; Pinnacle infrastructure maintenance represented a comparatively modest ongoing operational cost. The October 2025 simultaneous-transmission demonstration — proving that PNT and standard 5G data services could coexist on NextNav's licensed spectrum using commercial network equipment — marked the culmination of the immediate NextGen R&D phase and the beginning of what management characterized as a commercialization-readiness period, pending FCC spectrum reconfiguration.

## The Standardization Paradox

NextNav's NextGen approach presents an unusual competitive-intelligence risk. Unlike TerraPoiNT's proprietary over-the-air waveform, NextGen relies on 5G Positioning Reference Signals specified in 3GPP Release 16 and extended through Releases 17 and 18 — publicly documented, openly standardized signal formats available to any vendor building 5G equipment. NextNav's claim on NextGen is not that the PRS waveform is proprietary; it is that the licensed spectrum on which those signals broadcast, and the receiver processing methods used to extract sub-meter positioning accuracy from them, belong to NextNav.

This architecture offers a genuine deployment advantage: because NextGen uses standardized 3GPP positioning methods, it integrates with commercial chipsets and network equipment from Qualcomm, Ericsson, and Nokia without requiring custom protocols. The October 2025 demonstration was conducted on commercial 5G equipment — not NextNav-specific hardware — which was precisely the point.

But standardization cuts in both directions as 5G NR positioning matures. 3GPP Release 17's enhanced positioning features, broadly supported by major carrier networks by 2025, substantially improved GPS-independent accuracy using existing licensed spectrum — without any interaction with NextNav's M-LMS licenses. If cellular network densification and Release 18 improvements continue closing the accuracy gap, the incremental value of NextNav's dedicated 900 MHz spectrum becomes harder to articulate to MNO customers considering a licensing fee. NextNav's IP moat in the NextGen era rests less on blocking competitors from building 5G positioning infrastructure and more on whether 900 MHz coverage, power, and in-building penetration characteristics are sufficiently superior to justify that fee — a question the FCC rulemaking, and the carrier negotiations that would follow it, will ultimately answer.

chapters.title: Six Risks That Could Unwind the $2 Billion Spectrum Bet
chapters.body:
## The Regulatory Cliff

Every risk facing NextNav traces back to a single dependency: a favorable outcome from the Federal Communications Commission on WT Docket No. 25-110. The company's April 2024 Petition for Rulemaking asked the FCC to reconfigure the 902–928 MHz band into a paired 5 MHz uplink ~~/ 10 MHz downlink structure plus an additional 5 MHz~~ ==at 902–907 MHz and 10 MHz downlink at 918–928 MHz== — yielding a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use license enabling 5G NR operations. The FCC progressed to a Notice of Inquiry in March 2025, and an NPRM was noticed to the Office of Management and Budget in early 2026. But the path from NPRM to Final Rule is measured in years, not months — and organized opposition has assembled around arguments that carry genuine legal and technical weight.

Apple, the NTIA, the Security Industry Association, WISPA, and the GPS Innovation Alliance filed comments opposing the petition, principally on interference grounds. Their case rests on the fact that the 902–928 MHz band currently hosts a dense ecosystem of unlicensed Part 15 devices — consumer electronics, industrial sensors, smart home systems — operating on the shared ISM allocation. Reconfiguring the band to award NextNav a 15 MHz exclusive flexible-use license would displace or constrain these incumbents across a heavily populated slice of spectrum. NTIA's opposition carries particular weight: as the agency responsible for federal spectrum users, its concerns about adjacency interference with government systems in the 902 MHz neighborhood could delay rulemaking or impose technical conditions that limit signal power levels in ways that undermine NextNav's business case. WISPA, representing wireless internet service providers that use 900 MHz for rural backhaul, argued that interference to fixed wireless deployments could harm connectivity in underserved markets — a politically sensitive objection in any regulatory proceeding.

Under M-LMS licensing rules, NextNav's existing Mobile Location and Monitoring Service licenses grant usage rights that are broad but not exclusive in the Part 15 sense; reconfiguration to a flexible-use regime requires the FCC to affirmatively clear or protect incumbents, and that process invites challenge at the D.C. Circuit. A final rule vacated on administrative grounds — or issued with signal-power restrictions that prevent coverage equivalent to GPS — would render the spectrum economically inert. Against a June 2028 convertible note maturity, any such delay is not merely inconvenient. It is potentially fatal.

## The AT&T Revenue Cliff

NextNav's current revenue base is, in practical terms, a single contract. [AT&T/FirstNet represented approximately 89% of Q3 2025 revenue](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1865631/000155485525000923/nn-20250630.htm), and the Pinnacle floor-level altitude service agreement — extended in October 2025 through October 2028 — generates virtually the entirety of the company's $4–6 million annual commercial income. The number has therapeutic value as a proof of deployability but negligible structural significance against a $70 million annual operating loss.

The risk is not that AT&T terminates abruptly. The risk is renegotiation. Should AT&T determine that evolving 5G NR positioning standards — built into handsets by Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek without any contractual dependency on NextNav — can satisfy FCC z-axis accuracy mandates at lower cost, the carrier holds considerable leverage at the October 2028 renewal. A step-down in contract value, a conversion from a network-operations fee structure to a per-call usage model, or a scope reduction to a subset of markets would each materially alter NextNav's already thin revenue profile. A renegotiated contract that reduces annual revenue by half — to approximately $2 million — would eliminate roughly $3 million from a cash burn calculation already running at $70 million per year. The math is unforgiving: the AT&T relationship is simultaneously the company's only meaningful commercial proof point and a single point of failure that the company has not diversified away from in more than a decade of operations.

## The June 2028 Maturity Wall

The $190 million of 5% senior secured convertible notes issued in March 2025, led by Fortress Investment Group affiliates and M-Cor Capital, come due in June 2028. The conversion price is $12.56 per share. As of the frozen snapshot, NextNav's 52-week trading range was approximately $10.84 to $24.19, implying the notes were alternately in and out of the money throughout the period. With approximately ~~95–100 million diluted shares outstanding~~ ==135.6 million common shares outstanding as of March 13, 2026==, full conversion of the notes would add roughly 15.1 million shares — dilution of approximately ~~15 percent~~ ==10 percent== — which, at current market valuations, transfers significant value from common stockholders to noteholders.

Cash and short-term investments stood at approximately $152 million as of December 31, 2025. Against an operating loss run rate of approximately $70 million per year, the liquidity runway to June 2028 is arithmetically tight: two and a half years of burn consumes approximately $175 million, implying a cash shortfall before maturity absent revenue growth or additional financing. If the FCC rulemaking has not advanced to Final Rule by mid-2027 — a plausible scenario given the procedural calendar — NextNav's ability to refinance the notes on favorable terms diminishes sharply. Capital markets for a company with $4–5 million in revenue, no domestic MNO licensing agreements beyond AT&T, and an unresolved FCC proceeding would price any new debt at rates materially above the current 5% coupon, if available at all. Dilutive equity issuance at prices near the conversion threshold remains the more probable outcome — but at the cost of significant shareholder impairment.

## Carrier Integration as the Second Regulatory Hurdle

FCC approval of spectrum reconfiguration is necessary but not sufficient. The NextGen platform requires mobile network operators to embed PNT capability into their 5G base stations — integrating NextNav's licensed-spectrum 5G PRS waveform into hardware and software stacks that carriers have spent years optimizing for throughput, not positioning. As of the frozen snapshot, NextNav had no domestic MNO licensing agreement beyond the AT&T Pinnacle relationship, which is a Pinnacle altitude service contract, not a NextGen platform license. The MetCom International agreement in Japan covers waveform technology licensing pending Japanese regulatory approval — commercially promising, but geographically and structurally distinct from U.S. carrier integration.

Large U.S. MNOs operate on multiyear infrastructure refresh cycles. Integration of a new PNT waveform requires Radio Access Network software updates, potentially new fronthaul configurations, and coordination with equipment vendors — Ericsson, Nokia, Samsung — whose own roadmaps determine the pace of feature adoption. Carriers with sufficient spectrum holdings may prefer to internalize positioning capability through in-house 5G NR implementations rather than licensing a third-party solution, particularly if 3GPP standards evolve to narrow the accuracy gap NextNav claims for its spectrum-enhanced approach.

## The Standards Erosion Risk

3GPP Release 16 introduced 5G NR positioning, and Release 17 expanded the toolkit with sidelink and reduced-capability device positioning. Major chipset manufacturers — Qualcomm, MediaTek, Intel — have been implementing these capabilities in commercial silicon without requiring dedicated licensed spectrum. NextNav's core technical claim is that broadcasting on ~~12 MHz of licensed lower 900 MHz spectrum~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering more than 90% of the U.S. population== at signal powers approximately 10,000 times stronger than GPS provides positioning accuracy and jamming resilience that standardized 5G NR cannot match. That gap is real today. Whether it remains durable through Releases 18 and 19 — as 3GPP adds further positioning enhancements, and as dense small-cell deployments improve 5G NR geometric diversity — is less certain. If commercial 5G NR positioning closes to sub-meter accuracy in outdoor and near-indoor environments, NextNav's spectrum-based differentiation narrows to highly specific use cases: deep indoor, GPS-denied, and high-security government environments. Those markets are real but not large enough to support a $2 billion equity valuation.

## The Fortress Problem

NextNav's governance structure concentrates risk in ways that create potential conflicts of interest at the precise moment they are most dangerous. Mariam Sorond holds both the CEO and Board Chair roles — an arrangement that removes a standard layer of independent oversight over management decisions, including capital allocation, executive compensation, and strategic alternatives. Fortress Investment Group and M-Cor Capital occupy simultaneously the position of largest debt holders — $190 million face value of convertible notes — and significant equity holders following their pre-IPO venture participation and post-SPAC equity accumulation.

The conflict embedded in this dual position becomes acute as June 2028 approaches. If NextNav enters 2028 with insufficient cash to repay the notes and insufficient share price appreciation to make voluntary conversion attractive at $12.56, Fortress faces a choice that is structurally adversarial to common shareholders: it can force repayment, triggering a liquidity event that wipes out equity, or negotiate a restructuring that preserves its creditor position at the expense of dilution or other concessions extracted from common holders. Fortress's incentives as an equity investor nominally align with common shareholders, but its senior secured creditor position gives it a superior claim in any downside scenario. The single-asset nature of NextNav's balance sheet — a spectrum license portfolio that is legally encumbered as collateral for the convertible notes — means there is no unencumbered asset base to support an independent recapitalization that does not flow through Fortress's consent. For common shareholders, that is the governance risk hiding in plain sight on the balance sheet.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Regulatory Calendar Runs the Clock

For most technology companies, the next twelve months are shaped by product cycles, sales pipelines, and margin expansion. For NextNav, the cadence is determined by Washington. Everything downstream — revenue, valuation, survival — traces back to a single regulatory progression: the Federal Communications Commission's conversion of WT Docket No. 25-110 from a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking into a Final Rule that grants NextNav's petition to reconfigure the lower 900 MHz band for 5G NR-based terrestrial PNT operations.

As of the frozen snapshot date in late May 2026, that progression is further advanced than at any prior point in NextNav's history — and still nowhere near complete.

## Quarter-by-Quarter Catalyst Timeline

**Q2 2026 (through June 30):** The pivotal near-term milestone is the formal publication of the NPRM in the Federal Register. The NPRM was noticed to the Office of Management and Budget in early 2026, a procedural prerequisite to publication; the typical lag from OMB notification to Federal Register publication has historically run two to five months, placing a plausible publication window in the April–June 2026 timeframe. Publication starts the comment clock — the standard public comment period for spectrum rulemakings is 30 to 60 days, with reply comments following 30 days later. ~~NextNav's Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in mid-May, will be the first opportunity for management to characterize the NPRM's proposed band reconfiguration language and frame whether it mirrors, narrows, or broadens the April 2024 petition.~~ ==NextNav's Q1 2026 earnings call, held in mid-May and reporting revenue of $995 thousand and a net loss of $10.6 million, was the first opportunity for management to characterize the NPRM's proposed band reconfiguration language and frame whether it mirrors, narrows, or broadens the April 2024 petition.==

**Q3 2026 (July–September):** If the NPRM published on schedule in Q2, the comment and reply comment periods close in Q3. This is historically the most intensive advocacy window: incumbents, interference-objectors, and support coalitions file thousands of pages of technical and economic submissions. Apple, the GPS Innovation Alliance, WISPA, and NTIA filed opposition comments at the NOI stage; those parties will likely file again with greater technical specificity at the NPRM stage. NextNav will need to respond substantively to interference modeling critiques. Any material narrowing of the proposed 15 MHz license — for example, a reduction to a smaller paired block, or geographic exclusions to protect incumbent operations — would constitute a partial defeat. The Q2 2026 earnings call, likely in early August, lands in the middle of this window.

**Q4 2026 (October–December):** The FCC's deliberative timeline post-comment-period is the most uncertain variable. A Final Rule in Q4 2026 would represent an extraordinarily fast processing cycle — roughly six months from NPRM to order — and is unlikely absent extraordinary political pressure or a streamlined proceeding. More plausibly, Q4 2026 sees the FCC commissioners and staff working through the record while NextNav pursues supplemental technical demonstrations and Congressional pressure campaigns. The October 2026 milestone that matters most is the second anniversary of the AT&T Pinnacle agreement extension — by then, Pinnacle renewal discussions for the post-2028 period may informally begin, a data point relevant to the long-term floor on Pinnacle revenue.

A secondary catalyst in this window is MetCom International. The December 2025 Japan licensing agreement is subject to Japanese regulatory approval; any announcement of regulatory clearance or pilot deployment in Tokyo or Osaka would validate the international licensing model and provide a commercial proof point independent of the U.S. rulemaking.

**Q1 2027 (January–March):** Full-year 2026 earnings are the first opportunity for investors to assess whether the Pinnacle revenue base stabilized or declined further, and whether operating expenditures — particularly the regulatory advocacy and R&D costs driving the $70 million annual operating loss — were maintained or reduced. At this point, NextNav will have consumed approximately $70 million more in cash from its year-end 2025 balance of $152 million, leaving roughly $80–90 million — approximately 12–15 months of runway against a June 2028 debt maturity that grows closer.

## Revenue and Loss Estimates: A Thin Consensus

NextNav's micro-revenue profile — $4.6 million in FY 2025, almost entirely from a single AT&T contract — does not attract the analyst coverage density that produces meaningful sell-side consensus estimates. The company trades on regulatory optionality, not earnings power, and the available research reflects that asymmetry.

| Period | Revenue Estimate | YoY Change | Operating Loss Estimate | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2026 | ~~$1.0–1.2M~~ ==$995K actual== | ~flat | ~~$(17–18M)~~ ==$(10.6M) net loss actual== | AT&T Pinnacle milestone timing |
| Q2 2026 | ~$1.0–1.3M | ~flat | ~$(17–18M) | AT&T Pinnacle; no new contracts assumed |
| Q3 2026 | ~$0.9–1.1M | ~flat/down | ~$(18–20M) | Single-customer concentration risk; Q3 seasonally softer |
| Q4 2026 | ~$1.1–1.5M | ~flat/up | ~$(17–19M) | Potential MetCom milestone payments or federal contract expansion |
| **FY 2026** | **~$4.0–5.1M** | **(13% decline to 11% growth)** | **~$(69–75M)** | No structural change without new carrier deals |

These estimates carry a critical caveat: they assume no new domestic carrier licensing agreements materialize before year-end 2026. A single MNO licensing event — a signed technology access or spectrum-sharing agreement with a Tier 1 U.S. carrier — would be non-recurring revenue that makes quarterly comparisons meaningless while dramatically resetting the forward revenue trajectory.

NextNav has provided no explicit revenue guidance for FY 2026, consistent with its practice of flagging only the qualitative shape of the Pinnacle revenue stream and the contingent nature of NextGen commercial revenue.

## What to Watch Each Quarter

The quantitative threshold that matters most in each earnings release is **cash and liquidity**: with $152 million at year-end 2025 and an operating cash burn rate of approximately $65–70 million annually, investors should track whether management's "beyond twelve months" runway guidance is maintained. A cash balance below $100 million entering 2027 shifts the capital structure conversation from deferred optionality to near-term refinancing necessity.

The operating metrics that confirm or break the thesis are:

- **FCC docket activity**: Number and identity of new support filers in WT Docket 25-110; any ex parte meetings between NextNav and FCC commissioners or staff; any change in FCC leadership posture toward the proceeding.
- **Carrier pipeline disclosures**: Any named or unnamed MNO "trials" or "integration discussions" mentioned in earnings commentary. The October 2025 5G simultaneous-transmission demonstration is the technical foundation; the commercial discussion that follows is the signal.
- **Federal government contract expansion**: The November 2023 unnamed federal agency contract for GPS/PNT characterization has not yet been described as generating material recurring revenue. Any disclosure of expanded federal scope — particularly from DoD or DHS — would represent a new revenue vector independent of the FCC proceeding.
- **MetCom deployment status**: Japanese regulatory approval and any news of pilot-network construction.

## Beat Versus Miss Framing

Given the binary-regulatory structure, "beat" and "miss" for NextNav are largely defined by the FCC timeline rather than by quarterly revenue deltas of a few hundred thousand dollars. That said:

A **beat quarter** looks like: Pinnacle revenue at or above $1.2 million, operating cash burn below $17 million, an NPRM published with proposed spectrum parameters broadly matching the petition, and a named MNO trial or integration announcement — any one of those last two would constitute a material positive surprise relative to current consensus positioning.

A **miss quarter** looks like: Pinnacle revenue below $900,000 (repeating the Q3 2025 trough), operating burn above $20 million, NPRM publication delayed into 2027, or — most damaging — any FCC staff language suggesting the proposed license structure will be materially narrowed or the proceeding bifurcated into separate interference and policy proceedings that add years to resolution.

## The Asymmetry at the Snapshot Date

The bull setup is stark in its simplicity: NextNav holds ~~12 MHz of licensed nationwide spectrum at 920–928 MHz~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous near-nationwide spectrum at 920–928 MHz covering more than 90% of the U.S. population, plus 4 MHz of complementary spectrum covering part of the U.S. population==, the FCC is actively conducting a rulemaking that could convert that spectrum into a 5G-capable national PNT license, and the company has approximately $80–90 million of liquidity runway into a June 2028 debt maturity that aligns the regulatory timeline. The [Brattle Group study](https://ir.nextnav.com) estimated $14.6 billion in total economic value from the reconfiguration. Even modest probability-weighting of that outcome at a fraction of current market capitalization implies significant upside from the May 2026 share price range.

The bear setup is equally unambiguous: $4.6 million in trailing revenue, $189 million in net losses, negative book equity, $190 million in convertible debt, a single customer representing nearly all commercial revenue, organized opposition from Apple and NTIA, and a regulatory timeline that has never delivered a Final Rule in fewer than 18 months from NPRM in a contested spectrum proceeding of this complexity. If the FCC issues an adverse ruling, narrows the license below commercial viability, or simply delays resolution past the June 2028 debt maturity, NextNav faces a recapitalization under duress.

The next twelve months are, in that sense, a patience trade with a hard clock: watch the docket, watch the cash, watch the carrier conversations — and understand that the catalyst that resolves the asymmetry is not in a quarterly earnings release but in a Federal Register notice whose publication date no one, including NextNav's management, can predict with precision.

chapters.title: The 2026–2030 Horizon: Three Scenarios for NextNav's Path from Spectrum Optionality to Operating Company
chapters.body:
The next three years compress NextNav's eighteen-year arc into a single legible test: does the regulatory and commercial scaffolding assembled between 2024 and early 2026 — the FCC Notice of Inquiry, the OMB-notified NPRM, the MetCom licensing deal, the October 2025 5G demonstration — convert into a functioning business before the June 2028 maturity of $190 million in convertible notes extinguishes management's room to maneuver? Three distinct paths run from where the company stands at the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026.

## Bull Case: Regulatory Acceleration and the Revenue Inflection, 2027–2030

The Bull Case hinges on the FCC issuing a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in the second half of 2026 — consistent with the OMB pre-notification disclosed in early 2026 — and publishing a Final Rule by late 2027 or early 2028 that reconfigures the lower 900 MHz band broadly as NextNav has petitioned, creating a nationwide 15 MHz flexible-use license for 5G NR-based terrestrial PNT.

Under this scenario, a Final Rule in hand transforms NextNav from a regulatory optionality play into a licensable infrastructure asset. Mobile network operators, already confronted with federal pressure to harden GPS-dependent timing infrastructure, face a procurement decision rather than a speculative one. Management has positioned the NextGen platform as an embedded carrier function — PNT signals delivered via standard 5G NR base stations on NextNav's spectrum — which means integration cost falls primarily on the MNO rather than on NextNav's balance sheet. If three or more domestic MNOs enter licensing agreements between 2027 and 2028, the revenue trajectory inflects sharply. Carrier licensing fees on a per-subscriber or per-base-station model — analogous to how spectrum overlay services are typically structured — applied to a combined addressable base of 200-plus million U.S. subscribers across three major networks implies annual licensing revenue potentially reaching the $50–$150 million range by 2029–2030, depending on fee structure, deployment pace, and the share of 5G sites activated with NextNav's PRS waveform.

Federal contract revenue provides a second leg. NextNav signed its first unnamed federal agency contract in November 2023 for GPS/PNT characterization services; the U.S. Department of Transportation's 2021 evaluation ranked TerraPoiNT first among all alternative PNT solutions tested. If Congress advances GPS resilience legislation — bipartisan interest has been consistent — and the executive branch designates TerraPoiNT or the NextGen platform as a critical infrastructure component under Space Policy Directive 7, federal procurement contracts for timing backup services at military bases, power grids, and financial exchanges could add a further $20–$50 million annually in high-margin federal revenue. The Pinnacle AT&T agreement, extended through October 2028, provides a continuing floor while these larger revenue streams develop. International royalties from MetCom and successor licensing deals could add $5–$20 million annually by 2030 if Japan deployment succeeds and two or three additional international markets follow. In aggregate, the Bull Case revenue envelope by 2029–2030 approaches $100–$250 million — a transformation that would, at prevailing SaaS-infrastructure multiples, support the existing market capitalization or higher without requiring any further equity dilution.

## Base Case: The Refinancing Gauntlet, 2027–2029

The Base Case assumes a more deliberate FCC process: the NPRM issues in 2027, meaningful opposition from Apple, NTIA, and incumbent 900 MHz device manufacturers prolongs the comment and reconsideration cycle, and a Final Rule does not arrive until 2028 or 2029. One domestic MNO executes a NextGen licensing agreement before year-end 2029, but widespread carrier adoption remains speculative through the forecast window.

The financial stress is structural. NextNav's operating cash burn at roughly $60–$70 million annually, against a cash position of approximately $152 million as of December 31, 2025, implies the company reaches a liquidity threshold in 2027 — precisely as the June 2028 convertible maturity looms. CFO Tim Gray, who managed a structurally analogous balance sheet at Anterix through multiple refinancing cycles, faces a narrow corridor: the company must either refinance the $190 million convertible before meaningful NextGen revenue materializes, execute at-the-market equity issuance into what may be a declining stock price if the FCC timeline slips, or secure a new debt facility on terms that a $4–5 million revenue company can realistically support.

Fortress Investment Group's dual position — as both equity investor and convertible noteholder — creates a potentially useful alignment: Fortress has a financial incentive to facilitate a recapitalization that preserves enterprise value rather than force a maturity default. But common shareholders bear the dilution cost of any rescue financing, and the $12.56 per-share conversion price embedded in the current notes sets a benchmark below which equity issuance becomes materially destructive. In the Base Case, the AT&T Pinnacle contract renewal in October 2028 provides the most important near-term credit metric — its renewal would signal continued commercial relevance and support refinancing conversations. Federal contract expansion provides modest upside but not enough to bridge the gap to self-sufficiency.

## Bear Case: Liquidity Crisis and the Distressed Asset Question

The Bear Case requires only two adverse developments that are individually plausible: the FCC denies the spectrum reconfiguration petition or issues a Final Rule so narrowly drawn — perhaps limiting the band to a geographically fragmented or power-constrained overlay — as to render commercial NextGen deployment economically nonviable; and AT&T declines to renew the Pinnacle agreement beyond October 2028.

Under this scenario, NextNav's revenue base essentially zeroes out. The Pinnacle service has no other operator of comparable scale, and the loss of the AT&T/FirstNet contract eliminates the single revenue stream that has defined the company's income statement since inception. The $190 million convertible cannot be refinanced at any viable cost of capital against a near-zero revenue company with contested spectrum assets. Fortress, as the largest noteholder, faces a recovery calculation: the spectrum licenses themselves — ~~12 MHz covering over 90 percent of the U.S. population~~ ==8 MHz of contiguous lower 900 MHz spectrum covering more than 90 percent of the U.S. population, plus a complementary 4 MHz block covering part of the U.S. population== — retain residual value as a passive spectrum holding, potentially $200–$400 million in a strategic sale to a larger carrier or private spectrum aggregator, but that value depends heavily on the FCC having at least issued an NPRM, which establishes the spectrum's potential utility even if the Final Rule has not arrived. A distressed sale to a Verizon, T-Mobile, or a private-equity spectrum aggregator in 2028–2029 would likely return par to convertible holders while wiping out common equity — ending NextNav as an independent company but not necessarily destroying the underlying spectrum asset.

## The International Hedge: Technology Licensing as a Sovereign Business

The MetCom agreement established a proof of concept that matters independent of the FCC outcome: NextNav's 5G PNT waveform and receiver IP can be licensed to international carriers operating in spectrum-permissive jurisdictions without requiring U.S. regulatory approval. Japan's metropolitan density — and its own GPS vulnerability concerns given regional geopolitical context — make it a natural first market. If MetCom's deployment succeeds technically and commercially, it creates a reference deployment that Europe, South Korea, Australia, and the Gulf states can evaluate.

A pure technology licensing model — royalties on waveform use and receiver chipset integration, independent of spectrum ownership — is structurally sustainable at small scale. Ten to fifteen international carrier agreements at $5–$15 million annual royalty each could generate $50–$200 million in high-margin licensing revenue without NextNav needing to own or operate any spectrum internationally. This pathway does not replicate the upside of the domestic Bull Case, but it constitutes a genuine standalone business that could service debt, sustain R&D, and support a smaller but solvent operating company — a meaningful floor in the Bear Case that pure spectrum optionality does not provide.

## Capital Allocation Framework: 2026–2027

Given the binary regulatory outcome, optimal capital allocation in the 2026–2027 window prioritizes optionality preservation across all three scenarios simultaneously.

| Priority | Action | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | International licensing acceleration | Revenue- and IP-positive in all scenarios; MetCom success accelerates deal flow |
| 2 | Federal contract pursuit | Non-FCC-dependent revenue; builds political constituency for spectrum rulemaking |
| 3 | R&D focus on receiver cost reduction | Lower integration cost accelerates MNO adoption under any regulatory outcome |
| 4 | Cash conservation vs. growth spending | Extend runway to 2028 maturity; defer discretionary spend until NPRM text is public |
| 5 | Refinancing preparation | Begin convertible refinancing dialogue in 2026 while cash position and market cap remain elevated |

The logic is straightforward: maximum optionality requires that NextNav reach the FCC Final Rule — whenever it arrives — as a solvent, commercially credentialed company with at least one functioning revenue stream beyond the AT&T Pinnacle floor. International licensing and federal contracts serve both financial and political purposes, demonstrating real-world deployment and building the coalition of government stakeholders whose support shapes FCC commissioner votes. Aggressive domestic R&D spending that does not translate into demonstrable progress risks burning cash needed for the refinancing cycle. The company that arrives at the FCC Final Rule with $75–$100 million in cash, one domestic federal contract, one validated international deployment, and a credible MNO licensing pipeline is a company with genuine leverage in the recapitalization negotiation — regardless of which scenario ultimately prevails.
